structure.section: Lead / unlabeled abstract (the gray box before Section I)
structure.purpose: Hooks with a vivid 'oracle' thought experiment, names the central concept (scientific understanding) as the 'essential aim of science,' poses ONE sharp framing question, then gives a full roadmap-in-miniature: where we look (philosophy + anecdotes), the three-dimension framework, and the aspirational payoff ('true artificial scientists'). Functions as a self-contained pitch.

Establishes stakes via a chain of provocative direct quotes from authorities (AI as 'new tool in the box,' 'revolutionizing science,' the chemical 'oracle'), then immediately introduces the counter-voice (skeptics who doubt AI yields understanding). States the paper's contribution (literature review + original survey of dozens of scientists' anecdotes), grounds it in a specific philosophical theory (de Regt & Dieks), previews the three dimensions, and ends with a mission statement ('put Scientific Understanding back to the limelight').

The definitional/framework-grounding core. Walks through the philosophy of science (Hempel's dismissal -> later formalizations -> de Regt & Dieks's contextual theory), justifies the chosen theory by ONE pragmatic strength (it is operationally testable via outcomes, not methodology), and restates the criteria in a set-off block. Builds the conceptual scaffolding everything later hangs on.

structure.section: III. What Is Next? (A. Beyond Re-Discovery; B. Beyond Discovery; C. Where to go from here?)
structure.purpose: A 'clearing the ground' / negative-definition section: rules out what does NOT count as understanding (rediscovering known laws; black-box discovery like AlphaFold) to sharpen the target. Uses concrete foils (heliocentrism, arrow of time, AlphaFold, hypothetical best battery material) to argue prediction/discovery are not the same as understanding, funneling to the real research question.

structure.section: IV. Three Dimensions of Computer-Assisted Understanding (A. Computational microscope; B. Resource of inspiration / artificial muse; C. Agent of Understanding)
structure.purpose: The substantive heart (~50%). Each dimension follows a repeated template: (1) define via a metaphor (microscope / muse / agent), (2) give 2+ concrete published examples of the CURRENT state, (3) a 'The future X' subsection projecting forward with named enabling technologies, (4) explicit open challenges. Dimensions are ordered by increasing autonomy/ambition, ending with the not-yet-existent 'agent of understanding' where the authors propose formal Conditions I & II and the 'Scientific Understanding Test.'

Short, forward-looking close. Restates the contribution in one breath, makes a single concrete recommendation (multidisciplinary collaboration of scientists + computer scientists + philosophers), and lands a bounded-but-bold aspirational claim ('within our lifetimes').

Crowdsources credibility (thanks ~40 named senior scientists, signaling the survey's reach), funding, figure credit. Five numbered footnotes carry caveats and edge-case hedges off the main line of argument.
structure.approxShare: ~7% text; references are a large share of page count

rhetoricalMoves: Open with a thought experiment ('Imagine an oracle that correctly predicts...') that dramatizes the gap between prediction and understanding before any jargon appears.
Distinguish the target concept by negation: dedicate whole subsections to what does NOT count (re-discovery, black-box discovery) so the positive definition is unmistakable.

Borrow external authority for the framework: anchor the entire piece on ONE named, award-winning philosophy-of-science theory (de Regt & Dieks, Lakatos Award) and justify the choice with a single operational virtue (testability).
Coin a unifying term ('androids') and explicitly footnote why ('focusing on the operational objective rather than the methodology'), letting the argument stay method-agnostic and future-proof.
Build a taxonomy of exactly three named, metaphor-labeled dimensions (microscope / muse / agent), declared 'dimensions' (independent, non-exclusive) and ordered by escalating ambition.
Use a strict repeated template per dimension: metaphor -> current real examples -> 'the future' projection -> open challenge, so the reader internalizes the pattern.
Pair every speculative claim with a concrete published citation of the current state, then a labeled honest gap ('As of now, we are not aware of cases like that').

Formalize the most speculative part: convert hand-waving about 'true AI scientists' into stated Conditions (I, II) and a named, Turing-test-style protocol ('The Scientific Understanding Test'), giving falsifiable structure to speculation.
Stage a believer-vs-skeptic dialectic early (enthusiasts' quotes vs. 'this excitement has not been shared among all scientists') to preempt objections and signal balance.
Set off key definitions, criteria, conditions, and the test in indented blocks so the load-bearing claims are visually scannable.
Bound the boldest claim with a time horizon ('within our lifetimes') rather than leaving it open-ended, making ambition feel disciplined.
Use a first-person-plural collective voice ('We are convinced,' 'We believe,' 'We hope') to assert a position while signaling it is a perspective, not a result.
genre.openingStrategy: A two-move opener. Move 1 (hook): a concrete thought experiment in plain language - an 'oracle' that perfectly predicts physics experiments, chemical reactions, protein function - immediately countered with 'we would not be satisfied... We want more,' which surfaces the paper's whole thesis (prediction is not understanding) without jargon. Move 2 (frame): elevates the topic ('frequently been recognized as the essential aim of science') and poses ONE crisp organizing question ('How can advanced artificial systems contribute to scientific understanding or achieve it autonomously?'). The second paragraph is a transparent roadmap that names the methods (philosophy of science + original anecdote survey), the three-dimension framework, and the aspirational endpoint. The reader knows the thesis, structure, and stakes within ~200 words.
genre.closingStrategy: A compact 'restate + recommend + aspire' conclusion. It (1) reaffirms the inevitability framing ('Undoubtedly, advanced computational methods... will further revolutionize'), (2) restates the unique contribution (connecting AI to the specific aim of understanding), (3) issues ONE actionable recommendation - cross-disciplinary collaboration among natural scientists, computer scientists, and philosophers of science, mirroring the paper's own method - and (4) closes on a deliberately bold but time-bounded vision ('within our lifetimes, transform androids into true agents of understanding'). The bookend returns to the 'essential aim of science' phrase from the opening, closing the loop. Future directions are not dumped at the end; they are woven throughout Section IV, so the conclusion stays short.
genre.figureUse: Three figures, all conceptual/schematic rather than data plots (appropriate for a Perspective). Figure 1 is a roadmap/overview that visually encodes the entire argument: inputs (literature + philosophy of science + scientists' anecdotes) -> the three dimensions -> a future roadmap; it doubles as a visual abstract. Figures 2 and 3 are each tied to a specific dimension ('The future computational microscope,' 'The future resource of inspiration') and visualize the FUTURE/speculative vision, not existing results - e.g., Fig 2 shows two projected advances (bigger compute via GPU/TPU/OPU/quantum, and multi-sensory data representation), Fig 3 enumerates five labeled inspiration sub-modes (A-E) that map directly to the prose subsections. Figures carry the speculative load and let the text stay citation-dense. No tables; the 'data' of the field lives in the 110 references and inline examples.
genre.toneNotes: Confident, evangelical, but disciplined. Heavy first-person plural ('We believe,' 'We are convinced,' 'We hope,' 'We envision') asserts strong positions while marking them as opinion. Hedging is deployed precisely where claims are speculative ('could,' 'might,' 'we expect,' 'admittedly futuristic,' 'we are not aware of cases like that') and withheld where the authors are firm. Notably honest about limits: repeatedly flags the third dimension as not-yet-existing and unobserved in their survey. Balanced via an explicit skeptic voice (Hoffmann & Malrieu's 'simulation vs. understanding' tension is cited). Footnotes absorb caveats (e.g., 'we leave aside whether the explanation is true or false'; 'our test is not clear-cut'). Speculation is high but always scaffolded by either a citation, a metaphor, or a proposed test - rarely free-floating. Voice is accessible and quote-rich, almost essayistic, reflecting Nature-family Perspective register rather than a dry review.
genre.lengthAndRefs: ~13 pages / roughly 6,000-7,000 words of main text (published as a Nature Reviews Physics Perspective, NRP 4:761-769). Abstract is a non-structured ~2-paragraph narrative lead (~250 words) that itself contains a thought experiment and a full roadmap - not a terse structured summary. 110 numbered references, very dense and current for 2022, mixing primary research (Nature/Science/PRL/PRX), philosophy-of-science books and papers (de Regt, Dieks, Hempel, Potochnik), and arXiv preprints (BERT, GPT-3, symbolic-regression work). 3 conceptual figures, 5 footnotes, 0 tables. Citation style is bracketed/numbered. Roughly half the word count is the Section IV taxonomy; references occupy a large fraction of total page count.
transferableLessons: Open your AI+energy Perspective with a concrete thought experiment, not a literature recap - e.g., 'Imagine a grid operator that can perfectly forecast every kilowatt of demand and generation...' then immediately name what's still missing (understanding/causal control/trust) to surface your thesis in plain language.

Anchor the piece on ONE crisp organizing question and a memorable framework of 2-4 named, metaphor-labeled categories (the way 'computational microscope / muse / agent' carries the whole paper). For AI+energy, candidates might be roles like 'optimizer / forecaster / co-designer / autonomous operator,' ordered by increasing autonomy.

Define by negation: spend a short section ruling out what does NOT count (e.g., black-box load forecasting that improves accuracy but yields no operational insight, or marginal efficiency gains that don't change the system) to sharpen what your contribution targets.

Borrow external authority for your framework - cite an established theory or taxonomy from energy systems / techno-economics / sustainability science and justify your choice with one operational virtue, exactly as they leaned on de Regt & Dieks.

Consider coining and footnoting a single umbrella term so the argument stays method-agnostic and doesn't date (their 'androids' move); this future-proofs the piece against churn in specific ML methods.

Use a strict repeated template for each category: metaphor/definition -> 2-3 concrete CITED present-day examples -> a 'the future' projection naming enabling technologies -> the key open challenge. Repetition makes a long middle section easy to follow.

Pair every speculative claim with either a real citation of the current state or a proposed concrete test, and explicitly flag honest gaps ('we are not aware of cases like that'). Speculation is credible only when scaffolded.

Formalize your most speculative ambition into stated conditions or a named evaluation protocol (their 'Scientific Understanding Test'); for AI+energy you might propose explicit criteria for, say, 'an autonomous grid agent that demonstrably understands.' This converts hand-waving into something falsifiable and quotable.
Put the speculative/forward-looking vision into conceptual figures (a visual-abstract roadmap as Figure 1, plus one schematic per category) so the prose can stay citation-dense and evidence-grounded.
Stage a believer-vs-skeptic dialectic early - quote both AI enthusiasts and credible critics - to preempt the 'AI hype' objection and signal balance to reviewers.

Keep the conclusion short: restate the contribution, give ONE actionable recommendation (e.g., a specific cross-disciplinary collaboration energy modelers + ML researchers + policy/economics), and bound your boldest vision with a time horizon ('within this decade') rather than leaving it open-ended.

Use confident first-person-plural voice ('we argue,' 'we envision') to own a clear position - a Perspective is expected to take a stance, not hedge into a neutral review - while hedging precisely on genuinely uncertain claims.
Set off your key definitions, criteria, and any proposed test/metric in indented blocks so the load-bearing claims are visually scannable.
Bookend: echo a signature phrase from the opening in the conclusion (they reused 'the essential aim of science') to give the piece a sense of closure.
Budget references generously and currently (~100+), blending primary research, a domain-foundational theory, and very recent preprints, so the Perspective reads as authoritative and up-to-the-minute.

structure.purpose: Title names the contribution as a stance or framework (GREENER 'principles', 'Why transparency matters', 'what this could mean for AI') rather than a neutral topic. A one-sentence standfirst/teaser previews the thesis. Signals genre = opinion essay, not survey.

3-4 move arc in a single paragraph: (1) state the opportunity/stakes, (2) name the problem/gap, (3) introduce the authors' framework or central claim by name, (4) state what the piece delivers (principles + best-practice guidance / a roadmap). No headings, no methods/results breakdown. iScience/Patterns add a 'Bigger Picture' box restating significance for a broad audience.

Hooks with a concrete, recent, quantified fact ('AI = 20% of data-center power by end 2024'; 'data centers could be 9% of global electricity by 2030'; 'Google AI use to exceed its current total by 2034'). Then states the gap (impacts under-quantified / under-reported / not yet standard practice) and ends with an explicit thesis sentence + a roadmap-of-the-article sentence. Establishes WHY NOW.

One or two sections that frame the issue and define scope (e.g., 'Unveiling the hidden sustainability costs'; 'Reducing computing's environmental footprint'; separate carbon vs water sections). Marshals existing evidence to make the problem feel urgent and tractable, setting up the framework.

structure.section: Core framework / central argument (the genre's centerpiece)
structure.purpose: Presents the authors' named, structured contribution: GREENER = 7 named principles each given a labeled mini-section; iScience = a phased transparency roadmap; Patterns = a bottom-up estimation method yielding ranges. Always organized, mnemonic, and reusable. This is the thesis made operational.

Translates the framework into practice: concrete tactics, regional case studies, sector analogies (healthcare/finance disclosure), or quantified scenario implications. Demonstrates feasibility and broad relevance, pre-empting the 'nice idea but impractical' objection.

Dedicated honest section naming opposing interests (operators' competitive/security concerns), data uncertainty, and the limits of the proposal ('transparency alone cannot solve everything'). Concedes, then reframes toward graduated/coordinated solutions. Earns credibility.

structure.section: Roadmap / future directions / conclusion + call to action
structure.purpose: Phased or staged forward look (iScience: Phase 1 2025-27, Phase 2 2027-30, Phase 3 2030-35), GREENER: 'Conclusion and next steps' with institutional adoption pathways. Ends with a normative call to action framing the change as a shared professional/policy responsibility, not optional.
Declaration of interests, author bio (Cell Press short-form), 28-75 references (lighter than a Review), supplemental info. Reference count is moderate and argument-supporting, not exhaustive.

rhetoricalMoves: Open with a single recent, quantified, attention-grabbing statistic to establish 'why now' (the timeliness hook)
Name the gap explicitly: impacts are under-measured, under-reported, or not yet standard practice
Coin or deploy a named, mnemonic, structured framework (GREENER acronym; 3-phase roadmap; bottom-up estimation) so the thesis is memorable and reusable
Use 'opportunity vs risk' framing - acknowledge AI's benefits before pivoting to its costs, so the critique reads as constructive not alarmist
Quantify with explicit ranges and uncertainty bands (32.6-79.7 Mt CO2; 4-20x overstatement) rather than false-precision point estimates
Steelman the opposition: state operators' competitive/security concerns or efficiency-optimism fairly before answering them
Concede-and-reframe: admit the proposal is necessary-but-not-sufficient, then position it as a prerequisite first step
Borrow legitimacy from other domains (graduated disclosure 'modeled on healthcare and finance')
Forward-project with staged timelines and named milestones to make the future feel actionable
Close with a normative call to action that reframes the behavior change as professional/policy responsibility shared by the reader
genre.openingStrategy: Every exemplar opens by establishing timeliness through a concrete, recent, quantified fact tied to a near-future inflection point (AI = 20% of data-center power by end 2024; data centers ~9% of global electricity by 2030; Google's AI electricity to exceed its current total by 2034; computational research emissions rising without sustainability practice). The hook is immediately followed by naming the gap (impacts insufficiently quantified / disclosed / standardized) and then a one-sentence explicit thesis plus a 'this Perspective will...' roadmap sentence. The opening answers WHY THIS, WHY NOW, and WHAT THE READER WILL GET, all within the first 1-2 paragraphs. Tone is urgent but measured, not catastrophist.
genre.closingStrategy: Conclusions are forward-looking and prescriptive rather than summarizing. The dominant device is a staged/phased roadmap with named time horizons (iScience: 2025-27 transparency, 2027-30 integration, 2030-35 net-zero AI) or an explicit 'next steps' section (GREENER) listing institutional adoption pathways. The piece ends on a normative call to action that reframes the recommended change as a shared responsibility (researchers, operators, policymakers) and a prerequisite for progress ('no straight path to transparency, but it is a prerequisite'). It concedes residual uncertainty while insisting the direction is clear and action cannot wait. Policy/disclosure mandates and collective mechanisms (consortia, public-private partnerships, reporting standards) are proposed as concrete vehicles.
genre.figureUse: Few, high-value display items (typically 2-3 figures, 0-1 tables; references moderate at ~28-75). Figures are conceptual/organizing rather than data-dense experimental results: (a) a hero schematic of the framework itself (the GREENER principles wheel; the data-gap taxonomy across operational/embodied/external domains); (b) a trend/projection chart establishing the urgency stat from the opening; (c) a roadmap/timeline figure visualizing the phased future-directions argument. Patterns uses data tables to present its estimation ranges transparently. Boxes are used for significance framing ('The Bigger Picture' in Cell Press) and to set off the named principles. The figures carry the argument's structure, not raw evidence.
genre.toneNotes: Authoritative but accessible; written for a broad cross-disciplinary readership, not specialists in one subfield. First-person and collective voice is used ('we argue', 'we propose', 'we call for') - explicitly opinion-bearing, which distinguishes Perspective from Review. Hedging is calibrated: confident on the thesis and direction, carefully hedged on numbers (consistent use of ranges, 'plausible pathways', 'significant uncertainty surrounds these figures'). Speculation about the future is permitted but always anchored to current data and labeled as projection/scenario, not prediction. Balance is achieved by genuinely conceding opposing interests and limitations before rebutting, which keeps the advocacy from reading as polemic. Normative/should-language is concentrated in the opening thesis and the closing call to action.
genre.lengthAndRefs: Short-to-mid length for the genre: GREENER (Nature Comp Sci Perspective) ~3,500-4,200 words with ~75 references and 2-3 figures; iScience Perspective ~8,500-9,000 words, ~30 references, 3 figures (incl. roadmap); Patterns short-form analytical piece ~5,500 words, 28 references, 5 data tables, 0 figures. Nature Methods long-form Perspective ~24 manuscript pages, 2 figures. Abstract is a single unstructured paragraph (~120-200 words) with no IMRaD sub-labels; Cell Press adds a 'Bigger Picture' significance box. Reference counts (28-75) are deliberately lighter than a Review and serve to support the argument rather than comprehensively survey. Nature-portfolio Perspectives typically run ~2,000-5,000 words of main text with 30-80 references and up to ~3-4 display items.
transferableLessons: Lead with one recent, quantified, near-future statistic that makes 'why now' undeniable, then immediately name the gap and state your thesis in one sentence - all within the first two paragraphs.
Make the abstract a single unstructured paragraph with a 4-move arc (stakes -> gap -> your named framework -> what the piece delivers); do NOT write an IMRaD abstract.

Build the whole essay around ONE named, mnemonic, structured framework (an acronym, a typology, or a phased roadmap). The framework is the deliverable and should get its own clearly labeled centerpiece section with parallel sub-parts.
Use the opportunity-then-risk framing: credit AI's benefits before critiquing its costs so your argument reads as constructive stewardship, not doom.
Quantify with explicit ranges and named uncertainty rather than point estimates; this is what earns trust in a forward-looking piece. State assumptions and where the numbers come from.

Devote a real, honest section to challenges, opposing interests, and the limits of your own proposal; then reframe ('necessary but not sufficient', 'a prerequisite') instead of dismissing - concession is a credibility-builder, not a weakness.
Borrow legitimacy by analogy to mature domains (e.g., disclosure norms in finance/healthcare) when proposing new norms.
End with a STAGED roadmap with concrete time horizons and named milestones, not a summary; conclusions must be prescriptive and forward-looking.

Close with a normative call to action that assigns shared responsibility across stakeholders (researchers, industry, policymakers) and names concrete vehicles (reporting standards, consortia, mandates).
Use first-person collective voice ('we argue/propose/call for') to mark the genre as opinion - this is the explicit license a Perspective gives you that a Review does not.
Keep display items few and conceptual: a hero framework schematic, an urgency/projection chart, and a roadmap timeline; let figures carry the argument's structure rather than raw data.
Keep references moderate and argument-serving (~30-75), and main text tight (~2,000-9,000 words depending on venue); a Perspective persuades, it does not exhaustively survey.

Choose a venue-appropriate length: Nature-portfolio Perspectives (e.g., Nature Computational Science) tend shorter and more principle-focused (~3,500-4,500 words); Cell Press Perspectives (iScience) allow a longer, roadmap-heavy treatment.
Pick a title that announces a stance or framework ('Why X matters', 'GREENER principles for...', 'what this could mean for...') rather than a neutral topic label.

structure.purpose: DEFINITION: 'Perspective articles are intended to provide a forum for authors to discuss models and ideas from a personal viewpoint. They are more forward looking and/or speculative than Reviews and may take a narrower field of view. They may be opinionated but should remain balanced and are intended to stimulate discussion and new experimental approaches.' Perspectives follow the SAME formatting as Reviews. WORD LIMIT: guideline 5,000 words (Reviews/Perspectives 'should not generally be more than 9 pages'; 5000 words + 4 display items + <=150 refs = ~9 pages). ABSTRACT: 200-word maximum preface that sets the stage and ends with a summary sentence (also used on PubMed/Medline, so include key words). REFERENCES: no more than 150. DISPLAY ITEMS: ~4 moderate display items (figures/tables/boxes); explanatory boxes welcomed. COMMISSIONED/PEER-REVIEW: most commissioned but unsolicited accepted via a synopsis (300-500 word background outline); peer-reviewed AND substantially edited by Nature's editors. DISTINCTIVE: Highlighted references - one bold sentence beneath each of the most important/relevant 5-10% of references explaining significance.
structure.approxShare: Highest-prestige, broadest target; ~5,000 words / 200-word preface / <=150 refs / ~4 display items

Perspectives may also advocate a controversial position or present a speculative hypothesis. Two articles advocating opposite sides in a research controversy are normally published as Perspectives.' structure.purpose: DEFINITION (from the official Perspective format-guide PDF): a Perspective is a scholarly, forward-looking discussion; format mirrors a Review but more opinionated/narrower. ABSTRACT: unstructured abstract, ideally 200 words maximum (minimal specialist detail, NO references, NO display-item citations). WORD LIMIT: 'follow word count recommendations as discussed with the editor' (no fixed cap; negotiated). REFERENCES: approximately 25 references per 1,000 words (i.e., scales with length). DISPLAY ITEMS: <=5 display items (tables, figures and boxes); boxes ideally 200-500 words; original display items preferred and schematics redrawn by in-house art editors. COMMISSIONED/PEER-REVIEW: effectively commission-led (file must be discussed with the editor) and peer-reviewed. DISTINCTIVE: MANDATORY/optional Key Points box (4-6 bullets, <=30 words each) - required on Nat Rev Bioeng, optional on many incl. Nat Rev Clean Technol, Nat Rev Electr Eng, Nat Rev Earth Environ; optional Glossary (one-sentence definitions); concluding summary section; continuous line numbers; structured manuscript checklist.
structure.approxShare: Most heavily editor-mediated and design-intensive; length editor-negotiated / ~25 refs per 1,000 words / <=5 display items / Key Points box

rhetoricalMoves: Shared template: Nature, Nature Energy, and Nature Sustainability use nearly identical 'personal viewpoint / more forward-looking and/or speculative than Reviews / may be opinionated but should remain balanced' language - so a Perspective is explicitly the portfolio's home for a thesis-driven opinion essay, not a neutral survey.

Controversy clause: Nature Energy and Nature Sustainability add 'Perspectives may also advocate a controversial position or present a speculative hypothesis. Two articles advocating opposite sides in a research controversy are normally published as Perspectives' - directly licenses a provocative 'export tokens not electrons' thesis.

Review-flavored variant: Nature Computational Science and Nature Climate Change cast the Perspective as a 'scholarly review/discussion of the primary research literature' that is too narrow or too controversial for a Review - so these expect more literature grounding and citation than a pure op-ed.

Commissioning reality: across the portfolio most Perspectives are commissioned/invited; unsolicited submissions are accepted but typically gated by a pre-submission synopsis (Nature: 300-500 word background outline; Nature Sustainability: explicit 1-2 page Synopsis-Perspective with an example figure and stated contribution).

Distinctive add-ons differ by venue: Nature requires bold one-sentence 'highlighted references' on the top 5-10% of citations; Nature Climate Change uses an annotated-key-citation analogue (<=10%); Nature Reviews uses a Key Points bullet box (4-6 bullets, <=30 words) plus optional Glossary and editor-redrawn conceptual figures.

Length/reference envelopes vary widely: shortest is Nature Energy (3,000 words / 50 refs), then Nat Comput Sci (4,000 / 100), then Nature, Nature Sustainability and Nature Climate Change (~5,000 words; 150 / 60 / 100 refs respectively); Nature Reviews has no fixed word cap (editor-negotiated, ~25 refs per 1,000 words).
genre.openingStrategy: Across all six venues the Perspective opening is expected to be an editor-facing, timeliness-driven hook: state why the topic matters and why it is timely now, then end the opening with a guiding paragraph that previews the article's argument. Nature/Nature Sustainability formalize this as a short preface (Nature 200-word preface ending in a summary sentence; Nature Sustainability 100-word unreferenced preface), and Nature Reviews requires an unstructured <=200-word abstract with no references that introduces the main themes for a broad readership. For an unsolicited 'export tokens not electrons' Perspective, the opening must be reverse-engineered into a pre-submission synopsis/outline that names the single central claim and its novelty.
genre.closingStrategy: BEST TARGET = Nature Sustainability, with Nature Energy as the strong runner-up and Nature Computational Science as the methodological alternative. Reasoning: (1) Topical home - the thesis ('stranded clean electricity should be exported as AI compute/tokens rather than as electrons') is fundamentally a sustainability/energy-systems and infrastructure-siting argument, which sits squarely in Nature Sustainability's and Nature Energy's scope. (2) Genre fit - both journals' Perspective definitions explicitly invite a forward-looking, opinionated, even controversial/speculative thesis and even pair opposing-side Perspectives, which matches a deliberately provocative claim. (3) Format headroom - Nature Sustainability allows up to 5,000 words, 6 display items and 60 references, enough room to build the techno-economic + policy + computational argument and to carry conceptual figures (e.g., a tokens-vs-electrons system diagram, a stranded-curtailment map, a cost-per-delivered-value comparison); Nature Energy is tighter (3,000 words / 50 refs / 6 items), better if the argument can be made crisply and energy-centrically. (4) If the paper's center of gravity is the AI/compute economics and modeling rather than energy policy, Nature Computational Science (4,000 words / 100 refs) is the better methodological venue. (5) Nature (main) is the highest-prestige stretch target (5,000 words, <=150 refs, highlighted references) but commissioning-dominated and demands the broadest cross-disciplinary significance; a Nature Reviews journal (e.g., Nat Rev Clean Technol / Nat Rev Electr Eng) is essentially commission-only and design-heavy, so realistic only via a pre-pitch to an editor. Recommended path: pitch a 1-2 page synopsis to Nature Sustainability first (it has the most explicit unsolicited-proposal route and the best topic+genre+length fit).
genre.figureUse: Conceptual/display-item norms by venue: Nature allows ~4 moderate display items including explanatory boxes and welcomes them; Nature Energy and Nature Sustainability allow up to 6 figures/tables (Nature Energy strongly encourages illustrations); Nature Computational Science and Nature Climate Change do not cap display items in the Perspective entry (defer to AIP/formatting). Nature Reviews caps at <=5 display items (figures/tables/boxes), strongly prefers ORIGINAL items, redraws schematics in-house, and allows 200-500-word explanatory Boxes plus a Key Points box. For an 'export compute not electrons' Perspective the highest-leverage display items are conceptual: a schematic contrasting the electron-export vs token-export value chains, a map/bar chart of stranded/curtailed renewable energy by region, and a comparison table of transmission losses + capex vs datacenter-sited compute economics.
genre.toneNotes: The portfolio explicitly sanctions a first-person, opinionated, forward-looking voice ('personal viewpoint', 'may be opinionated', 'forward looking and/or speculative', 'may advocate a controversial position or present a speculative hypothesis') - but every venue couples this with 'should remain balanced', 'briefly indicate opposing viewpoints', and 'should not be focused on the author's own work'. So the required register is confident-but-balanced advocacy: a clear thesis, acknowledged counterarguments (e.g., grid-export and interconnection counter-cases), and accessible language with specialist terms defined. The review-flavored venues (Nat Comput Sci, Nat Clim Change) expect the opinion to be anchored in the primary literature rather than asserted, and Nature emphasizes accessibility for nonspecialists. All Perspectives are peer-reviewed, so the speculative claim must be defensible, not merely rhetorical.
genre.lengthAndRefs: Comparison of caps (word limit / abstract / references / display items): Nature ~5,000 words, 200-word preface, <=150 refs, ~4 display items, highlighted-reference sentences on top 5-10%. Nature Energy up to 3,000 words, up to 50 refs, up to 6 figures/tables. Nature Sustainability up to 5,000 words, 100-word unreferenced preface, up to 60 refs, up to 6 figures/tables. Nature Computational Science up to 4,000 words, up to 100 refs (display items unspecified in entry). Nature Climate Change 3,000-5,000 words, up to 100 refs, annotated key citations on <=10% (display items unspecified in entry). Nature Reviews family: word count editor-negotiated (no fixed cap), ~25 refs per 1,000 words, <=5 display items (figs/tables/boxes), ideally 200-word unstructured abstract, plus Key Points box (4-6 bullets, <=30 words each) and optional Glossary. All Perspectives are peer-reviewed; nearly all are commission-led with an unsolicited-proposal/synopsis route.
transferableLessons: Pick the venue by scope first, then format headroom: for 'stranded clean power as AI tokens', Nature Sustainability (5,000 words / 60 refs / 6 items) and Nature Energy (3,000 words / 50 refs / 6 items) are the natural homes; Nature Computational Science is the alternative if the AI/compute modeling is the core.

Lead with the unsolicited-proposal route, not the full manuscript: budget a 1-2 page synopsis (Nature Sustainability explicitly requires Synopsis-Perspective with topics, organization, an example figure even as a sketch, key recent refs, and a one-line statement of the novel contribution; Nature wants a 300-500 word background outline). Editors gate these formats.

Frame the thesis to match the journal's own license for controversy: cite that Perspectives 'may advocate a controversial position or present a speculative hypothesis' - the 'export compute not electrons' claim is exactly the kind of provocative-but-balanced thesis these formats invite.

Stay within the tight reference budget by using highlighted/annotated references: Nature wants bold one-sentence significance notes on the top 5-10% of refs; Nature Climate Change wants short annotations on <=10%; plan citations selectively rather than exhaustively.

Design 2-4 original conceptual figures up front (value-chain schematic, stranded-energy map, electrons-vs-tokens cost/loss comparison) - display-item caps are 4-6 across these venues and original conceptual figures are preferred; if targeting a Nature Reviews journal, expect in-house redrawing and a mandatory/optional Key Points box (4-6 bullets, <=30 words).

Keep the front matter short and keyword-rich: a 100-200 word unreferenced preface/abstract that states the single central claim and ends with a summary sentence (Nature notes the preface is indexed on PubMed/Medline).

Write balanced advocacy in accessible, non-jargon prose, explicitly engaging counterarguments (grid interconnection, transmission build-out, datacenter water/siting limits) - all Perspectives are peer-reviewed and 'should remain balanced' and 'not be focused on the author's own work'.

facts.topic: Yarlung Tsangpo (Yarlung Zangbo) / Medog lower-reaches mega hydropower project, Tibet: specifications, power-evacuation difficulty, and west-China stranded clean power context

findings.claim: Planned total installed capacity of the Yarlung Zangbo / Medog project (world's largest hydropower facility on completion)
findings.source: Wikipedia (Medog Hydropower Station); China State Council / english.www.gov.cn; Enerdata

findings.claim: Expected annual electricity generation (about 3x the Three Gorges Dam; enough for ~300 million people / roughly the entire UK)
findings.source: Chinese government (english.www.gov.cn); Wikipedia; Xinhua via multiple outlets

findings.claim: Total planned investment (figure most consistently cited; early reports said >1 trillion yuan / ~US$137bn, later official figure 1.2 trillion yuan / ~US$167–170bn)
findings.value: 1.2 trillion yuan (~US$167 billion); some sources 1 trillion yuan (~US$137 billion)
findings.source: Chinese government announcement (Li Qiang ceremony); Reuters/Xinhua reporting; CRU Group

findings.claim: Approval date by the Chinese government
findings.source: Radio Free Asia; Wikipedia

findings.claim: Construction start date (groundbreaking ceremony in Nyingchi led by Premier Li Qiang)
findings.source: Chinese government (english.www.gov.cn); Wikipedia

findings.claim: Project structure: a cascade of five hydropower stations developed by Power Construction Corp of China (PowerChina); commercial operation expected ~2033 (some estimates 2035–2040 for full build-out)
findings.source: Wikipedia; ourchinastory.com; CRU Group

findings.claim: Location: Medog County, Nyingchi (Nyingtri) Prefecture, Tibet Autonomous Region, near the border with India's Arunachal Pradesh, at the Yarlung Tsangpo Great Bend around Namcha Barwa
findings.source: Wikipedia; The Diplomat

findings.claim: Terrain / hydraulic head: the river drops ~2,000 m (some sources 2,000–2,350 m) over a ~50 km span at the Great Bend, exploited by drilling four ~20 km tunnels through Namcha Barwa mountain. Water-energy density ~7x Three Gorges; canyon ~3x deeper than the Grand Canyon
findings.value: ~2,000 (range 2,000–2,350) drop over ~50 km; four ~20 km tunnels
findings.source: Wikipedia; Baiguan/The Diplomat analysis

findings.claim: WHY power is hard to use locally — local demand gap: Tibet is vast and sparsely populated with installed capacity only ~3–3.5 GW and 2024 generation only ~12–13 TWh, i.e. local demand is far below the project's ~300 TWh/yr output, so most power must be exported east
findings.value: Tibet capacity ~3–3.5 GW / generation ~12–13 TWh vs project ~300 TWh/yr
findings.source: Baiguan analysis; ourchinastory.com; tourtraveltibet.com overview of TAR electricity

findings.claim: WHY power is hard to evacuate — distance to load centers: eastern China consumption centers are >2,000 km away, requiring new ultra-high-voltage (UHVDC, e.g. ±800kV up to ±1100kV) lines under the West-East Power Transmission program; the existing central-Tibet 500kV interconnection already required 2,738 km of lines and is called the world's hardest grid project
findings.value: >2,000 km to eastern load centers; UHVDC ±800–1100kV needed
findings.source: smartelecmfg analysis; SASAC/China Daily (central Tibet grid 2,738 km); CRU Group

findings.claim: WHY hard — remoteness: the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon is one of the most inaccessible places on Earth; road access only arrived with the Paizhen–Medog highway in 2022, and an estimated 40 million tons of cement must be hauled in
findings.value: Road access since 2022; ~40 million tons cement to transport
findings.source: Baiguan / The Diplomat analysis

findings.claim: WHY hard — seismicity: site sits on the Indus–Yarlung suture / Eastern Himalayan Syntaxis near Namcha Barwa, one of the world's most seismically active zones; the 2017 Ms 6.9 Milin/Nyingchi quake triggered >1,820 landslides and 7 dammed (barrier) lakes in the Tsangpo gorge. Tunnels are reportedly designed to withstand magnitude up to 8.5
findings.value: Ms 6.9 (2017) caused >1,820 landslides + 7 dammed lakes; design to M8.5
findings.source: Springer Landslides journal (Milin earthquake); Baiguan/The Diplomat (M8.5 design)

findings.claim: Context — China national renewable curtailment rose sharply: H1 2025 solar curtailment 6.6% (vs 3.9% H1 2024) and wind 5.7% (vs 3.0%); national curtailment cap was relaxed from 5% to 10%
findings.source: China National New Energy Consumption Monitoring & Early Warning Centre, via Power Technology

findings.claim: Context — west-China stranded clean power is acute regionally: Tibet wind curtailment hit 30.2% (from 2.3%) and solar 33.9% (from 5.1%) in H1 2025; Qinghai solar curtailment 15.2% (from 8.8%); biggest volume losses in Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia, Gansu, Qinghai
findings.source: Power Technology citing China National New Energy Consumption Monitoring & Early Warning Centre

findings.claim: Context — economic value of curtailed/wasted renewable generation; absent curtailment and other losses, H1 2025 wind+solar output would have been ~13% higher
findings.source: Power Technology; Ember China Energy Transition Review 2025

facts.caveats: Numbers vary by source and report date. (1) Installed capacity is most often given as 60 GW but some outlets cite up to 70 GW; annual generation of ~300 TWh is consistent across sources. (2) Investment: early (Dec 2024) reports said "over 1 trillion yuan (~US$137bn)"; the July 2025 groundbreaking figure is widely reported as 1.2 trillion yuan (~US$167–170bn). USD conversions differ with exchange-rate assumptions. (3) Completion year of ~2033 is an estimate; full multi-station build-out may extend to 2035–2040. (4) The >2,000 km distance to eastern load centers and the specific UHV line plan (±800kV vs ±1100kV) come from analytical/industry sources, not an official transmission plan, which has not been publicly detailed — hence medium confidence. Tibet's local capacity/generation figures (~3–3.5 GW / ~12–13 TWh) are approximate and drawn from secondary overviews. (5) Curtailment statistics trace to China's National New Energy Consumption Monitoring and Early Warning Centre as relayed by Power Technology, Ember, and Carbon Brief; the US$17bn lost-value figure is an estimate and varies by methodology. (6) Several useful primary pages (e.g., the 2026 Diplomat piece, power-technology) intermittently returned 403/paywall, so some figures were corroborated via search snippets rather than full-text fetch. (7) The project is geopolitically sensitive (downstream Brahmaputra concerns in India/Bangladesh) and official Chinese disclosures are limited, so some technical details remain unconfirmed by independent verification.

facts.topic: Economics of long-distance electricity transmission, focused on China's UHVDC west-to-east lines (distance, losses, capital cost, levelized cost adder, converter stations, and utilization effects)

findings.claim: Typical UHVDC west-to-east line distances range from ~1,400 km to ~3,300 km. Examples (all ±800 kV unless noted): Yunnan-Guangdong 1,438 km; Xiangjiaba-Shanghai 1,907 km; Jinping-Southern Jiangsu 2,059 km; Hami-Zhengzhou 2,210 km; Gansu-Zhejiang 2,370 km; Changji-Guquan (Zhundong-South Anhui, ±1,100 kV) 3,293-3,324 km (world's longest).
findings.source: Wikipedia: Ultra-high-voltage electricity transmission in China

findings.claim: Changji-Guquan is the world's first ±1,100 kV UHVDC line: 3,324 km, rated 12,000 MW (12 GW), rated current 5,455 A. It gives ~50% more capacity than ±800 kV links. ABB/Hitachi supplied converter equipment under a contract of over USD 300 million (one supplier's scope).
findings.source: NS Energy / ABB news / Power-technology (Changji-Guquan project)

findings.claim: UHVDC line losses are commonly cited at roughly 3-3.5% per 1,000 km for ±800 kV class; some sources quote 2-3% per 1,000 km for the highest-voltage UHV lines. Higher voltage (1,100 kV) lowers current and loss for the same power.
findings.source: Pictet Asset Management / saurenergy / allpcb (HVDC AC vs DC loss summaries)

findings.claim: For the Xiangjiaba-Shanghai ±800 kV line (~1,907-2,000 km), total transmission losses were reported as under 7%, materially lower than the prior 500 kV system. This is the headline end-to-end transmission figure (line plus a few percent for the two converter stations).
findings.source: ABB / Power Technology (China Leads the Way in Low-Loss Power)

findings.claim: Implied total losses over a typical 2,000-3,000 km UHVDC corridor: roughly 6-10% end-to-end. This combines ~3-3.5%/1,000 km line loss (so ~6-10% over 2,000-3,000 km) plus ~0.6-0.7% per converter station (two stations). Note a US 500 kV HVDC modeling study (lower voltage) found ~12.9% loss over 1,000 miles (~1,600 km), illustrating how lower voltage sharply raises losses.
findings.value: ~6-10 end-to-end over 2,000-3,000 km (vs ~13% for 500 kV/1,600 km)
findings.source: iScience / NREL 'Cost of long-distance energy transmission by different carriers' (PMC8661478)

findings.claim: Total installed capital cost of a recent ±800 kV UHVDC project (Gansu-Zhejiang): RMB 35.3 billion (~USD 4.82 billion) for 8,000 MW capacity over 2,370 km. This implies ~USD 603 per kW of capacity for the whole link (line + both converter stations), or ~USD 0.25/W per 1,000 km.
findings.source: Transformer Magazine (China begins work on $4.82B transmission line)

findings.claim: Converter (terminal) stations are roughly one-third of total UHVDC project cost; a pair can reach on the order of USD 1 billion. For the Changji-Guquan ±1,100 kV link, the Changji converter station alone had a total investment of RMB 8.05 billion (~USD 1.2 billion) on a 630-acre site. ABB's single-supplier converter equipment scope for that link exceeded USD 300 million.
findings.value: ~1/3 of project cost; Changji station RMB 8.05B (~$1.2B); ABB scope >$300M
findings.source: ABB news / NS Energy / Transformer Magazine

findings.claim: Benchmark converter station unit cost from a 3,000 MW ±500 kV LCC-HVDC study: ~USD 301 million per terminal, i.e. ~USD 100/kW per station (~USD 200/kW for the pair). LCC-HVDC (used in China's UHVDC) has the lowest converter cost of HVDC types due to cheap thyristors.
findings.source: ResearchGate / MDPI Processes (HVDC LCC cost breakdown, 3,000 MW ±500 kV)

findings.claim: Levelized transmission cost adder for long-distance HVDC: a peer-reviewed estimate puts it at ~USD 41.5/MWh per 1,000 miles (~USD 0.041/kWh per ~1,600 km), i.e. roughly USD 0.025-0.03/kWh per 1,000 km. Industry analysis cites ~2-7 cents/kWh per 1,000 km, and that a 3-10 cents/kWh transport spread is needed for a 10% IRR on a ~1,000-mile cable.
findings.source: iScience/NREL (PMC8661478) and Thunder Said Energy HVDC economics

findings.claim: For China specifically, sending power east via UHV (vs shipping coal east to burn it) is estimated to lower delivered cost by ~0.03-0.08 yuan/kWh (~0.4-1.1 US cents/kWh), indicating the transmission adder is small relative to generation cost and competitive with coal-by-rail logistics.
findings.source: Power Engineering International (UHV transmission goes the distance in China)

findings.claim: Capacity factor / utilization is the dominant driver of per-kWh transmission cost: because the line capex is fixed, halving utilization roughly doubles the per-kWh cost. China's first three UHV lines (commissioned 2009-2012) reached only 21% to 56% utilization of design capacity in 2014, well below the ~80-100% assumed in cost models, which inflates real per-kWh transmission cost and revenue recovery for grid owners.
findings.source: South China Morning Post (China's under-utilised ultra-high-voltage power lines)

findings.claim: Cost models for HVDC transmission typically assume 100% utilization, which the authors note is 'unlikely for real-world application' - so published levelized adders (e.g. ~4 cents/kWh per 1,000 miles) are lower bounds; at 50% utilization the effective per-kWh transmission cost roughly doubles. UHVDC becomes economic only beyond ~1,000 km, with ~1,500-1,600 km cited as the breakeven vs lower-voltage HVDC.
findings.value: 100% utilization assumed (vs ~50% real) → ~2x per-kWh cost; economic >1,000 km
findings.source: iScience/NREL (PMC8661478) and Thunder Said Energy

findings.claim: Renewable content and curtailment context: only ~one-fifth of electricity carried on China's UHV lines was wind/solar (share roughly flat since 2021); the 14th Five-Year Plan required new UHV corridors to carry at least 50% renewables. Low renewable share and variability constrain utilization and the clean-energy value of the lines.
findings.value: ~20 (renewable share of UHV throughput); 50% policy minimum for new lines
findings.source: Dialogue Earth (Done right, China's UHV grid can help phase out coal)

facts.caveats: Several precise figures are derived or approximate. (1) Loss rates: a frequently quoted "1.5% per 1,000 km" for Changji-Guquan appears in one secondary source and conflicts with the more standard 3-3.5%/1,000 km for ±800 kV; I treat the 3-3.5% range as the reliable engineering figure and 2-3% as the optimistic UHV claim. The "<7% over 2,000 km" for Xiangjiaba-Shanghai is a well-cited ABB-origin figure but blends line and converter losses. (2) Capital cost: $603/kW for Gansu-Zhejiang is my own division of the reported $4.82B total by 8 GW capacity (whole-link, including both converter stations); it is not a normalized $/kW-km from the source. The cleaner US-study figures ($1,502/mile-MW capital; $41.5/MWh-1,000mi levelized) are for a ±500 kV system and over-state losses relative to ±800/1,100 kV UHV, so they bracket rather than match Chinese UHVDC. (3) Converter station costs mix sources: the ~$100/kW LCC benchmark is from a 500 kV study; the Changji station's RMB 8.05B is a single-terminal Chinese figure and includes site/land. (4) The per-kWh levelized adder (2-7 cents/1,000 km) is broad and IRR/utilization-dependent; the China-specific 0.03-0.08 yuan/kWh is a coal-substitution saving estimate, not a strict levelized transmission tariff, hence low confidence. (5) Utilization figures (21-56%) are from 2014 for the earliest lines; utilization has reportedly improved since but remains a known weak point, and current line-by-line capacity factors were not obtained from a primary source (Dialogue Earth and MDPI full texts returned HTTP 403). The central economic point is robust across sources: UHVDC line capex is largely fixed, so the per-kWh transmission cost scales roughly inversely with utilization/capacity factor.

facts.topic: LCOE of large hydropower; scale of stranded/curtailed renewable energy worldwide; and computing (esp. Bitcoin mining) as a flexible, location-agnostic, interruptible load to monetize stranded/curtailed power

findings.claim: Global weighted-average LCOE of newly commissioned hydropower in 2024
findings.source: IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024

findings.claim: Global weighted-average LCOE of newly commissioned hydropower in 2023 (fell 7% from USD 0.061/kWh in 2022)
findings.source: IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2023 (Executive Summary)

findings.claim: Weighted-average LCOE of large hydropower added over the past decade in China and Brazil (well below global average; China's low-cost resource and scale drive down the global figure)
findings.source: IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2023

findings.claim: Global weighted-average total installed cost of new hydropower projects (2022 figure; basis for 2023 decline)
findings.source: IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2023 (Executive Summary)

findings.claim: China was the largest hydropower market in 2023, accounting for ~44% of global hydropower additions, driving down the global weighted-average cost
findings.source: IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2023
