findings.source: IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024

findings.claim: Lazard LCOE+ reference points for context (US, unsubsidized): combined-cycle gas turbine rose to $76/MWh in 2024; nuclear ~$182/MWh
findings.source: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+) June 2024 (v17.0)

findings.claim: China national renewable curtailment: solar curtailment rate H1 2025 vs H1 2024 (NEA data via Bloomberg); wind curtailment also rose. National utilization floor relaxed from 95% to 90% (curtailment ceiling raised from 5% to 10%) in 2025.
findings.source: Power Technology / Bloomberg (citing China NEA)

findings.claim: West China extreme regional curtailment: Tibet wind curtailment 30.2% (2025, from 2.3% in 2024), Tibet solar 33.9% (from 5.1%); Qinghai solar 15.2% (from 8.8%). Western provinces with the largest projects can exceed 30%.
findings.value: Tibet wind 30.2%, Tibet solar 33.9%, Qinghai solar 15.2%
findings.source: Power Technology (citing China NEA)

findings.claim: Estimated scale of recoverable curtailed/under-utilized renewable energy in China: nationwide inter-provincial coordination could raise effective renewable penetration by ~99.88 TWh, equal to ~9.1% of total solar+wind generation (proxy for the magnitude of stranded/curtailed potential).
findings.source: Bloomberg coverage of China grid coordination study

findings.claim: ERCOT (Texas) wind and solar curtailment due to grid congestion in 2024 (West zone: 3.1 TWh wind + 2.2 TWh solar curtailed)
findings.source: Modo Energy, The Curtailment Crisis: Saving wind and solar investments in ERCOT

findings.claim: ERCOT curtailment rates 2022: 5% of available wind and 9% of available utility-scale solar curtailed; projected to rise to ~13% (wind) and ~19% (solar) by 2035; congestion and supply-demand mismatch are the main drivers
findings.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Today in Energy

findings.claim: Chile renewable curtailment (vertimiento): ~1.5 TWh solar curtailed in 2023, rising to 5.9 TWh of solar+wind in 2024 (~121% increase). Driven by Atacama oversupply and limited north-to-south transmission.
findings.source: pv magazine International / Ember

findings.claim: Chile cumulative curtailment value: ~11,900 GWh (~11.9 TWh) of renewable electricity curtailed Jan 2022-May 2025, representing an estimated US$562 million in lost revenue
findings.source: pv magazine International (citing Chilean market data / Ember)

findings.claim: Concept/precedent: Bitcoin mining as a location-agnostic, interruptible, price-responsive load that acts as a 'buyer of last resort' for stranded/curtailed power; Proof-of-Work has no data-locality requirement so it can co-locate at flare sites or stranded wind/solar farms and consume only otherwise-wasted energy.
findings.source: Bitcoin Magazine / VALR / industry analyses

findings.claim: Peer-reviewed precedent (Texas): modeling study found Bitcoin mining could absorb the large majority of curtailed Texas wind energy and turn it into profit. Reported result: ~93% of curtailed wind energy utilized to generate ~$239 million profit (using 2020-2021 ERCOT curtailment data).
findings.value: ~93% of curtailed wind captured; ~$239 million profit
findings.source: Niaz, Liu, You, 'Can Texas mitigate wind and solar curtailments by leveraging bitcoin mining?', Journal of Cleaner Production, Vol. 364 (2022), DOI 10.1016/j.jclepro.2022.132700

findings.claim: ERCOT controllable/flexible-load precedent: large flexible load program established in 2022; nearly all operational large flexible load (>75 MW rated) is Bitcoin mining. Miners curtail >95% of usage during peak/scarcity and are paid demand-response credits.
findings.value: program since 2022; flexible loads >75 MW; >95% curtailment during peaks
findings.source: Hashrate Index / Baker Botts (ERCOT large-load analysis)

findings.claim: Real-world monetization precedent: Texas paid Bitcoin miner Riot Platforms ~$31.7 million in August 2023 to curtail (~$24.2M power-curtailment credits + ~$7.4M demand-response), illustrating revenue from acting as an interruptible load during grid stress.
findings.source: CNBC (citing Riot Platforms / ERCOT)

findings.claim: Flared-gas precedent (Crusoe Energy 'Digital Flare Mitigation'): scaled to >250 MW across 7 US states and Argentina; deployed >110 mobile generation systems; abated >39 billion cubic feet of gas; ~99% methane combustion vs open flares; division sold to NYDIG in March 2025.
findings.value: >250 MW; >39 Bcf gas abated; ~99% methane reduction
findings.unit: MW capacity; Bcf gas; % methane reduction
findings.source: Crusoe Energy newsroom / Contrary Research / DCD

findings.claim: Generalization of flexible load beyond crypto: utilities could add ~126 GW of new (AI/cloud/computing) load with minimal grid expansion if loads accept curtailment averaging ~1%/yr (short-duration, <~50 hours/yr) - supporting computing as a broadly flexible, interruptible load.
findings.unit: GW new load addable at ~1% curtailment tolerance
findings.source: Duke University Nicholas Institute 'Rethinking Load Growth' (cited via IEA/industry coverage)

facts.caveats: Definitions and confidence: (1) LCOE — IRENA's global hydro figure (USD 0.057/kWh = ~$57/MWh in both 2023 and 2024) is high-confidence from the primary source's executive summary text; the China/Brazil large-hydro figure of ~USD 0.040/kWh (~$40/MWh) is medium-confidence because I extracted it from a search synthesis of the full IRENA report rather than reading the report table directly (IRENA PDFs would not parse via fetch). Note IRENA LCOE excludes integration/grid costs; Lazard's US figures use different financing/scope and are not directly comparable to IRENA's global weighted averages. (2) Curtailment — China rates are well-sourced as percentages, but a robust national absolute-TWh figure for curtailed renewables in 2024 was not found in a single authoritative primary source; the ~100 TWh 'recoverable' figure is a study-derived proxy (low confidence) and conflates curtailment with broader under-utilization. China also has a separate hydropower-curtailment problem (transmission-constrained spillage in Yunnan/Sichuan in wet years, documented academically e.g. Renewable Energy 2018), distinct from the 2022 drought-driven hydro *shortage* — I did not find a clean recent TWh number for hydro spillage specifically. ERCOT 2024 '>8 TWh' is from Modo Energy (analyst, medium confidence); EIA 2022 percentages are high confidence. Chile figures come from pv magazine/Ember (medium). (3) Computing-as-flexible-load — the Texas Bitcoin study's headline numbers (~93% of curtailed wind utilized; ~$239M profit) come from a peer-reviewed paper (J. Cleaner Production 2022) but the exact figures were captured from search summaries because ScienceDirect full text was paywalled/403; treat the specific $239M/93% as medium confidence pending full-text verification. Crusoe operational metrics are company-reported (medium). Many crypto-mining 'green'/grid-benefit claims originate from industry-aligned sources and are contested (e.g., MIT CEEPR and other work questions net climate benefit); the physical fact that mining is interruptible and location-agnostic is well established, but the magnitude of net benefit is disputed. Dates: searches run May 2026; some 2025/2026 figures reflect partial-year or preliminary data.

facts.topic: Stranded hydropower exported as "canned/congealed electricity": aluminum smelting (Iceland, Norway, Quebec, US Pacific Northwest) as the 20th-century precedent for AI tokens as 21st-century embodied electricity

findings.claim: Primary aluminum smelting (Hall-Heroult electrolysis) is extremely electricity-intensive: roughly 13-16 kWh of electricity per kg of aluminum; best modern smelters ~13 kWh/kg, world average closer to 15 kWh/kg.
findings.source: Wikipedia (Aluminium smelting) citing 14-16 MWh/tonne; Alcoa figures via MrReid.org / Stanford PH240

findings.claim: Expressed per tonne, the canonical figure is 14-16 MWh (14,000-16,000 kWh) of electrical energy per tonne of primary aluminum; a commonly cited US/industry value is ~14,800 kWh per metric ton, and the International Aluminium Institute tracks AC/DC power per tonne with global averages declining toward ~14,000 kWh/t.
findings.source: International Aluminium Institute (Primary Aluminium Smelting Power Consumption); Wikipedia; industry sources

findings.claim: Electricity is the dominant cost in aluminum smelting, typically cited as ~40% of total production cost (range ~20-40% across sources and regions). This is why aluminum is nicknamed 'congealed electricity'.
findings.unit: percent of production cost from electricity
findings.source: The Conversation ('congealed electricity'); Fastmarkets / discoveryalert; ArcticToday/Yale E360 (20-40%)

findings.claim: Aluminum is explicitly nicknamed 'congealed electricity' because power is ~40% of its production cost and smelting is so energy-intensive it has historically driven dedicated power plant construction. (This is the direct precedent for the 'canned electricity' framing.)
findings.source: The Conversation (Australia aluminium tax incentives article)

findings.claim: Smelters are deliberately sited at sources of cheap, often stranded, hydroelectric power because the process uses huge continuous power and smelting is 'economical only if there are inexpensive sources of electricity'; plants locate close to large (often hydro) power stations to hold down cost.
findings.source: Wikipedia (Aluminium smelting)

findings.claim: Economic value density of aluminum as 'canned electricity': at ~14,500 kWh/tonne embodied and an LME aluminum price of ~$2,600/tonne (2025), the product is worth only about $0.18 per kWh of embodied electricity. (Range: ~$0.14-0.20/kWh across $2,100-2,900/t and 14,000-16,000 kWh/t.)
findings.unit: USD of product per kWh of electricity embodied
findings.source: Author calculation from LME aluminium price (alcircle/AluminiumChina) and IAI/Wikipedia energy intensity

findings.claim: LME primary aluminum cash price was ~$2,300/tonne (2024 average) and rose to ~$2,640-2,900/tonne through 2025 - the numerator for the value-per-kWh calculation.
findings.source: AL Circle / AluminiumChina (LME aluminium price trend)

findings.claim: Iceland: built large hydro/geothermal to export stranded energy as aluminum because it has no grid interconnection to Europe. First smelter opened ~1969 (Straumsvik, ISAL, by Swiss Alusuisse), tied to a 210 MW hydro plant on the Thjorsa; Karahnjukar (690 MW, 2007-09) was built specifically to power an Alcoa smelter.
findings.value: 1969 first smelter; 690 MW Karahnjukar dam for one smelter
findings.source: Wikipedia (Energy in Iceland); Yale E360; ArcticToday

findings.claim: Iceland's aluminum smelters consume the majority of national electricity - about 70% of generation circa 2005-2013 and roughly 64% of demand in more recent (2023) data; ~13 TWh of ~17 TWh total. Power-intensive industry (mostly aluminum) is the de facto export channel for otherwise stranded electricity.
findings.unit: percent of Iceland electricity to aluminum/power-intensive industry
findings.source: Wikipedia (Energy in Iceland / Electricity sector in Iceland)

findings.claim: US Pacific Northwest: aluminum was the first major industrial customer of Columbia River hydropower. Bonneville Power Administration signed its first contract with Alcoa in Dec 1939 (smelter near Vancouver, WA, opened 1940). Industry grew to 10 smelters, ~11,000 jobs, consuming 3,150 average MW.
findings.value: 1939 first contract; 10 smelters; 3,150 avg MW; ~11,000 jobs
findings.source: Northwest Power and Conservation Council (Columbia River History: Aluminum)

findings.claim: By the mid-20th century the Pacific Northwest produced ~40% of US aluminum (and 6-7% of world capacity), enabled by Bonneville hydro rates roughly half what competitors paid (e.g. New Kensington, PA private utilities charged industry at least double BPA rates in 1940).
findings.value: ~40% of US output; rates ~half of competitors'
findings.source: Northwest Power and Conservation Council; BPA history (HistoryLink / nwcouncil)

findings.claim: Pacific Northwest smelters declined as cheap power vanished: BPA raised rates ~250% between 1979 and 1983; by the 2000-2001 West Coast energy crisis all 10 smelters were shut down or at minimal production. Demonstrates the model collapses when the underlying electricity stops being cheap/stranded.
findings.source: Northwest Power and Conservation Council (Columbia River History: Aluminum)

findings.claim: Quebec: Alcan acquired Saguenay River hydro sites as the foundation of its smelting empire; by the 1970s Alcan owned 6 hydro stations (~2,015 MW avg) and was the only producer in the world able to expand capacity 30% without raising power costs. Cheap, plentiful hydro is described as Quebec's permanent competitive advantage in aluminum.
findings.value: 6 hydro stations; ~2,015 MW; +30% expansion without higher power cost
findings.source: The Globe and Mail (Quebec aluminum); Hydro-Quebec / Alcan (Wikipedia, Canadian Encyclopedia)

findings.claim: Norway (Norsk Hydro): aluminum smelting grew directly out of harnessing waterfalls - Hydro's Sam Eyde bought the Rjukan waterfall in 1902. Today Hydro runs ~40 hydro plants delivering ~13.7 TWh/yr, dedicated largely to smelting; Norway supplies ~40% of Europe's aluminum with a carbon footprint ~75% below the global average.
findings.value: Rjukan waterfall 1902; ~40 plants; 13.7 TWh/yr; 40% of EU aluminum
findings.source: Norsk Hydro ('Power of power' history; Norway operations); Wikipedia (Norsk Hydro)

findings.claim: Remote stranded-hydro smelters are built where electricity literally cannot be sold to a grid: e.g. Rio Tinto's Kitimat (BC) is powered by the dedicated Kemano hydro plant (Nechako reservoir, 16 km tunnel, ~1,000 MW, 80 km line to the smelter) - power monetized only by converting it to shippable metal.
findings.value: Kemano ~1,000 MW dedicated; 16 km tunnel; 80 km transmission line
findings.source: CIM Magazine (Rio Tinto Kitimat); Bechtel (Kitimat modernization)

findings.claim: Threshold economics confirming the 'export-stranded-power-as-metal' logic: viable smelting generally needs electricity below ~$40/MWh on 10+ year contracts; regional power tariffs ~$20/MWh (Middle East), $35-40/MWh (US/Europe), ~$55/MWh (China) per CRU - so only places with cheap/stranded power can profitably 'can' electricity into aluminum.
findings.source: CRU via Light Metal Age / discoveryalert (US aluminum smelting economics)

facts.caveats: Value-per-kWh ($0.18/kWh) is my own arithmetic (LME price / energy intensity), not a directly published statistic; it varies with metal price ($2,100-2,900/t) and intensity (14,000-16,000 kWh/t), giving roughly $0.13-0.21/kWh. Note this is GROSS value embodied, not margin - the smelter pays for the power, alumina, anodes, labor, so net value-added per kWh is far lower. The electricity cost share '~40%' is a widely repeated industry rule of thumb (range 20-40% by region/price era) rather than a single audited figure; I could not access the live IAI data tables (definition pages only) or the paywalled ArcticToday article, so the precise current global average energy intensity (~14,000 kWh/t) is taken from secondary sources and Wikipedia's 14-16 MWh/t range rather than a fetched primary IAI value. Iceland's industry-share figures span 64-72% depending on year and whether measured against generation or demand. The AI-token analogy half of the framing (tokens as 21st-century 'canned electricity') is the user's thesis: I gathered the aluminum precedent rigorously, but a clean apples-to-apples 'USD of AI output per kWh' figure is genuinely uncertain - rough public estimates suggest frontier LLM inference can embody electricity at a vastly higher value density than aluminum (often cited as dollars-to-hundreds-of-dollars of service value per kWh vs aluminum's ~$0.18/kWh), but those AI numbers are model-, price-, and use-case-dependent and were not the focus of these aluminum-specific sources. Treat the AI value-density comparison as directional, not precisely sourced. Several supporting figures (Norsk Hydro plant counts, Kemano specs) come from company/secondary sources and may reflect slightly different base years.

facts.topic: AI datacenter energy economics and energy cost per token of frontier LLM inference

findings.claim: Datacenter-level energy per output token, optimized production frontier inference (Epoch AI bottom-up estimate, GPT-4o-class MoE ~100B active params, H100, 500 output tokens, 10% utilization, 70% power, datacenter overhead folded into 1500W/GPU). 0.3 Wh/query = 0.6 mWh/token = ~2.2 J/output token; equivalently ~0.6 Wh per 1000 tokens and ~1.7 million output tokens/kWh.
findings.source: Epoch AI (Gradient Updates: How much energy does ChatGPT use?)

findings.claim: Per-query energy for optimized frontier-scale inference (>200B-param model, H100 8-10 GPU nodes, 500 input + 300 output tokens, PUE modeled log-normal P5-P95 1.05-1.40, node power 0.7x of 11.3-14.1 kW max). Peer-reviewed bottom-up median 0.34 Wh/query (IQR 0.18-0.67); on a 300-output-token basis this is ~1.1 mWh/token ≈ ~4 J/output token (includes 500-token input prefill).
findings.unit: Wh per query (≈ 4 J per output token incl. prefill)
findings.source: Joule / Microsoft Research (Energy Use of AI Inference: Efficiency Pathways and Test-Time Compute)

findings.claim: Defensible RANGE for datacenter-level energy per output token across model sizes, batching, and prompt regimes: best-case well-batched serving ~0.7-2.4 J/token (≈1.7-5 million tokens/kWh); typical mixed production ~2-10 J/token; worst-case large-context/low-batch or reasoning ~20-70+ J/token. Aggregate frontier upper-bound estimates of 40-60 kWh per million tokens imply ~17,000-25,000 tokens/kWh.
findings.unit: Joules per output token; tokens per kWh
findings.source: Arthur Clune (per-token energy costs) + Antarctica.io One-Token Model + Epoch AI

findings.claim: Energy per token is highly sensitive to batching and prompt size. On 4xH100, large 16k-input prompts cost ~36-72 J/token at batch 1 (10-20 kWh/M tokens) but drop to ~9.6-19 J/token at batch 8; a single H100 at batch 512 (small prompt) reaches ~2,174 tokens/sec at ~0.69 J/token. Demonstrates a 25-100x spread driven by batch size and context length.
findings.source: Arthur Clune (Another look at per-token energy costs)

findings.claim: GPU output throughput for Llama 2 70B under batched serving (MLPerf Inference v4.1, offline): NVIDIA DGX H100 (8 GPUs) delivered 24,525 tokens/sec total, i.e. ~3,066 output tokens/sec per H100. H200 systems reach ~33,000 tokens/sec (8 GPUs), ~40% higher than H100.
findings.source: NVIDIA / MLCommons MLPerf Inference v4.1

findings.claim: Single-GPU LLM serving throughput ranges widely: ~250-300 tokens/sec for interactive single-stream 13B-70B serving, up to thousands of tokens/sec aggregate under large batches (e.g. Mixtral 8x7B reached ~21,000 tokens/sec at batch 1024 with FP8; GPT-OSS-120B ~1,009 tokens/sec on one H100 via vLLM). Throughput depends on batch size, quantization (FP8), and engine (vLLM/TensorRT-LLM).
findings.source: NVIDIA Technical Blog (TensorRT-LLM, Mixtral 8x7B) / BytePlus (GPT-OSS-120B vLLM)

findings.claim: GPU power (TDP): NVIDIA H100 SXM5 = 700 W; H100 PCIe = 350 W; H100 NVL = 350-400 W/GPU. H200 SXM = 700 W (same power envelope as H100 SXM, higher memory/bandwidth). Full DGX/HGX node max power draw ~11.3-14.1 kW for 8-10 H100 (incl. CPUs, networking, NVSwitch); per-GPU all-in (server+overhead) commonly modeled at ~1,400-1,700 W.
findings.source: NVIDIA H100/H200 datasheets; Joule/Microsoft Research node modeling

findings.claim: Datacenter PUE: industry average ~1.54-1.56 (Uptime Institute 2024-2025 surveys). Hyperscalers achieve 1.09-1.20. Google reported a fleet-wide trailing-12-month PUE of 1.09 in 2024.
findings.source: Uptime Institute Global Data Center Survey 2024 / Statista 2025

findings.claim: Achievable PUE in cold/high-latitude climates: Google's lowest trailing-12-month campus PUE was 1.09 (Hamina, Finland and Belgium), aided by ~2C average ambient and seawater free-cooling. Cold-climate free-air cooling can run 8-10 months/year (vs 3-4 months in temperate climates). The Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact set a 1.3 annual PUE target for new facilities in cool climates by 2025.
findings.source: Google Data Centers (Efficiency / Hamina); Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact

findings.claim: AI datacenter capex: ~$38 million per MW one-time ($38 billion for a 1 GW facility) for a typical US facility using NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 servers. Annualized total cost of ownership ~$8.5 million/MW/yr ($8.5 billion/yr for 1 GW), assuming 5-yr server and 14-yr facility lifespans.
findings.source: Epoch AI (Total cost of ownership of a one-gigawatt AI data center)

findings.claim: Cost-structure share of an AI datacenter (annualized TCO of a 1 GW facility, ~$8.5 billion/yr): servers & networking (chips/GPUs) ~$5.0 billion = ~60%; facility & infrastructure ~$2.6 billion = ~29%; energy/electricity only ~$0.6 billion = ~7%; other OpEx ~4%. Hardware vastly dominates; electricity is a minor (~7%) share. (Industry-wide, McKinsey estimates ~60% of total AI datacenter investment flows to chip/compute hardware makers.)
findings.source: Epoch AI cost breakdown; McKinsey (The cost of compute)

findings.claim: Test-time scaling (reasoning) sharply raises per-query energy: queries ~15x longer than typical lift median energy ~13x to 3.91-4.32 Wh (IQR ~2.2-7.4 Wh). Conversely, non-production / academic estimates can overstate real per-query energy by 4-20x versus production-scale serving.
findings.source: Joule / Microsoft Research (Energy Use of AI Inference)

facts.caveats: Major assumption dependencies: (1) Energy-per-token figures depend heavily on whether they count GPU-only vs full-node vs datacenter (PUE-adjusted) energy, and on output-only vs input+output tokens. The Epoch AI ~2.2 J/token and Joule ~0.34 Wh/query figures are bottom-up estimates for optimized production serving of MoE models with ~100B active parameters; smaller dense models (7B-70B) and worst-case low-batch/long-context serving can be 10-100x different, so the tokens/kWh range (~17,000 to ~5,000,000) is genuinely wide and not a single number. (2) These are estimates/benchmarks, not metered production telemetry from frontier labs (which is largely undisclosed); the Joule paper explicitly notes that prior non-production estimates overstated energy by 4-20x. (3) GPU throughput numbers (e.g., 3,066 tok/s/H100 on Llama-2-70B) are MLPerf offline-scenario, FP8/optimized; real interactive serving with latency SLAs yields lower per-GPU throughput and thus higher J/token. (4) The 0.3 Wh ChatGPT figure was corroborated by OpenAI and Google leadership but remains an external estimate. (5) Capex/cost-share figures are from Epoch AI's GB200-based model for a US facility; actual $/MW varies materially with location, power deals, chip generation (Blackwell vs Hopper), and server lifespan assumptions (3-yr life raises TCO to ~$12B/GW/yr; 7-yr lowers it to ~$7B/GW/yr). The ~7% electricity share is an annualized-cost share and is sensitive to electricity price (modeled near $0.15/kWh) and utilization; at very high power prices or low hardware cost it would rise. (6) The Joule/arXiv PDF could not be parsed directly; its numbers were taken from the abstract and a literature-review summary, and minor version differences exist between the arXiv preprint (median 0.34 Wh, test-time 4.32 Wh) and the published Joule abstract (median 0.31 Wh, test-time 3.91 Wh).

facts.topic: Global scale of AI token consumption and AI compute energy outlook (2024–2030)

findings.claim: Google processes over 3.2 quadrillion tokens per month across all its surfaces (Gemini, Search/AI Overviews, YouTube, Workspace, Cloud APIs, multimodal), a ~7x jump year-over-year, announced by CEO Sundar Pichai at Google I/O 2026 (May 2026).
findings.source: Google (Sundar Pichai I/O 2026 keynote, blog.google)

findings.claim: Google's monthly token throughput trajectory across its surfaces: ~9.7 trillion/month (May 2024), ~480 trillion/month (May 2025), >3.2 quadrillion/month (May 2026) — roughly 330x growth over two years.
findings.source: Google I/O 2026 keynote (via blog.google); cross-reported by Cryptobriefing/Shacknews

findings.claim: Earlier in the cycle (Sept/Oct 2025), Google reported processing 1.3 quadrillion tokens/month across all services, showing the steep mid-2025 to mid-2026 ramp toward 3.2 quadrillion.
findings.source: PYMNTS (citing Google)

findings.claim: OpenAI's API platform processes over 6 billion tokens per minute, announced by Sam Altman at DevDay on Oct 6, 2025 — up ~20x in under two years (from ~300 million tokens/min). This equals ~8.64 trillion tokens/day, ~259 trillion/month, ~3.15 quadrillion/year.
findings.source: OpenAI DevDay 2025 (Sam Altman keynote), reported via TechCrunch/The Neuron and Tibor Blaho

findings.claim: Industry-wide estimate: the total LLM API market processes approximately 50 trillion tokens/day, or ~1.5 quadrillion tokens/month (multi-source analysis of provider API telemetry, enterprise surveys, platform data; published Nov 19, 2025). This implies ~18 quadrillion tokens/year for the API market.
findings.source: Fireworks.ai ('State of Agent Environments')

findings.claim: OpenRouter empirical usage study analyzed over 100 trillion tokens of real-world LLM interactions over a 13-month rolling period ending Nov 2025 (single aggregator platform); useful as a lower-bound real-usage dataset and for usage-mix shifts (open-source share rose to ~1/3; reasoning models exceeded 50% of usage by late 2025).
findings.source: OpenRouter 'State of AI 2025' / arXiv 2601.10088

findings.claim: Derived annual global token estimate (method below): API-market floor ~18 quadrillion tokens/yr (Fireworks 50T/day x 365); broader all-surface estimate is materially higher — Google's surfaces alone imply ~38 quadrillion/yr (3.2e15 x 12). A reasonable 2025–2026 global all-provider, all-surface band is ~20–50+ quadrillion tokens/year and rising several-fold annually.
findings.source: Derived from Fireworks.ai (API market) and Google I/O 2026 (all surfaces)

findings.claim: Frontier-model output pricing (premium tier) spans roughly $25–$180 per million output tokens; e.g., Claude Opus 4.6 at $5 input / $25 output, GPT-5.4 Pro at $30 input / $180 output per million tokens (2026).
findings.source: IntuitionLabs / TLDL LLM API pricing comparisons; provider pricing pages

findings.claim: Mid-tier model pricing roughly $3–$15 per million output tokens; e.g., GPT-5.4 $2.50/$15, Claude Sonnet 4.6 $3/$15, Gemini 2.5 Pro ~$1.25 input per million tokens (2026).
findings.source: IntuitionLabs / TLDL LLM API pricing comparisons

findings.claim: Cheap/budget model pricing is roughly $0.40–$3 per million output tokens, with input as low as $0.10–$0.14 per million; e.g., DeepSeek-V3 $0.14 input / $0.28 output, Gemini 2.0 Flash $0.10 input / $0.40 output, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite $0.10 input per million tokens. Industry prices fell sharply (some report ~80% drops 2025→2026).
findings.source: DeepSeek API docs; Google Gemini API pricing; pricepertoken/TLDL

findings.claim: IEA: global data-centre electricity consumption was ~415 TWh in 2024 (~1.5% of global electricity) and is projected to roughly double to ~945 TWh by 2030 in the Base Case (~just under 3% of global electricity). Source: IEA 'Energy and AI' report, April 2025.
findings.source: IEA, 'Energy and AI' (Apr 2025), Executive summary / Energy demand from AI

findings.claim: IEA: electricity use by AI-optimised (accelerated) servers is projected to grow ~30% per year in the Base Case and to more than quadruple by 2030; AI is the single largest driver of data-centre demand growth. US and China account for ~80% of global data-centre demand growth to 2030 (US +~240 TWh / +130%; China +~175 TWh / +170%).
findings.source: IEA 'Energy and AI'; S&P Global summary

findings.claim: IEA high-demand ('Lift-Off') scenario: global data-centre electricity demand in 2035 could be ~45% higher than the Base Case, exceeding 1,700 TWh and reaching ~4.4% of global electricity demand.
findings.source: IEA, 'Energy and AI'

facts.caveats:
Definitional inconsistency is the biggest issue. Provider token figures are not apples-to-apples: Google's 3.2 quadrillion/month is "across all surfaces" (includes Search/AI Overviews and heavy multimodal image/video/audio tokenization), whereas OpenAI's 6B tokens/min and the Fireworks 50T/day figure are API/inference-platform numbers. Multimodal tokens (a single image can be hundreds-to-thousands of tokens) inflate "all-surface" counts relative to text API traffic, so summing across providers risks both double-counting (e.g., OpenRouter routes to the same providers) and category mismatch.

Date context: today is 2026-05-30. Google I/O 2026 (May 2026, 3.2 quadrillion/month) and OpenAI DevDay 2025 (Oct 6, 2025, 6B tokens/min) are the latest primary figures. The 1.3 quadrillion Google figure is an earlier-2025 number, consistent with the 480T (May 2025) → 3.2Q (May 2026) ramp.

Annual global token method: (a) API-market floor = Fireworks 50T/day x 365 ≈ 18 quadrillion/yr; (b) all-surface upper estimate anchored on Google alone (3.2e15 x 12 ≈ 38 quadrillion/yr) plus other providers suggests a 2025–2026 band of ~20–50+ quadrillion tokens/yr globally. This is a synthesis, not an official statistic — confidence is low, the band is wide, and it is growing several-fold per year (Google ~7x YoY; OpenAI ~20x in two years), so any single annual number is quickly outdated.

Pricing caveats: pricing changes monthly and many "frontier" prices were cut sharply (Anthropic Opus 4.1 $15/$75 → Opus 4.6 $5/$25; reported ~80% industry-wide drops 2025→2026). Some pricing specifics (e.g., GPT-5.4/5.2 family, Gemini 3 Flash) come from third-party aggregators (IntuitionLabs, TLDL, pricepertoken), not always confirmed against the provider's live pricing page at fetch time; treat exact per-model cents as indicative. Cached/batch/context-window tiers and per-token discounts are not reflected.

Energy caveats: IEA 'Energy and AI' (April 2025) Base Case (~945 TWh by 2030) is one scenario among several; ranges across analysts (Goldman, Morgan Stanley, McKinsey) for 2030 data-centre demand vary widely (roughly 700–1,300+ TWh). "Data-centre" electricity is broader than "AI" alone, though IEA attributes the bulk of growth to AI/accelerated servers. The IEA report predates the most recent (late-2025/2026) token-throughput surges, so actual buildout may track the upper scenarios. I could not directly fetch the IEA executive-summary or S&P pages (timeout/403); the 415 TWh (2024), 945 TWh (2030), and Lift-Off >1,700 TWh (2035) figures were confirmed from the official IEA 'Energy demand from AI' page.

verdicts.claim: The Yarlung Tsangpo / Medog hydropower project has a planned installed capacity of about 60 GW and expected annual generation of about 300 TWh.
verdicts.bestEstimate: Installed capacity: ~60 GW (60,000 MW) as the most-cited planned figure, though credible estimates range up to ~70-81 GW depending on how many of the cascade stations and how much of the ~70 GW technically-exploitable Great Bend potential is captured. Expected annual generation: ~300 TWh/year (300 billion kWh), i.e. roughly 3x the Three Gorges Dam (~22.5 GW / ~95-112 TWh).
verdicts.reasoning: The claim's two headline numbers are consistently reported across independent sources (Wikipedia, Power Magazine, CNN, The Diplomat, Jamestown, and Chinese-language outlets including Guancha and Xinhua-derived reporting). The project (officially the Motuo/Medog Hydropower Station on the lower Yarlung Tsangpo / Brahmaputra) broke ground 19 July 2025, costs ~RMB 1.2 trillion (~USD 167-170 bn), uses a diversion-tunnel scheme through the Great Bend with five cascade stations, and targets ~2033 first operations. Two caveats prevent a stronger 'exact' framing: (1) China has NOT published a single official, definitive total capacity number — the project is described as secretive, so '~60 GW' is the most common figure but several reputable analyses cite 'more than 60 GW' or a 60-80 GW range (e.g., Jamestown: '60-80 GW' for the lower reaches; multiple sources: 'as high as 70 GW'; the basin's main-stream theoretical potential is ~80 GW and the Great Bend's technically exploitable potential ~70 GW). So '~60 GW' is best read as a conservative/lower-bound planned figure, not a hard cap. (2) The 300 TWh/year figure traces to Chinese reporting (China Energy News 2021; Ta Kung Pao 2025) and is the widely repeated 'triple Three Gorges' number; sources do not transparently reconcile it with the exact final capacity. Internal consistency check: 300 TWh / (60 GW x 8760 h) implies a ~57% capacity factor, which is physically reasonable for a high-head diversion hydro plant (at 70 GW it implies ~49%, also reasonable). Because the claim says 'about 60 GW' and 'about 300 TWh,' it accurately reflects the dominant planned figures; it is only mildly oversimplified in that capacity could ultimately be higher (up to ~70-81 GW) and no number is officially confirmed.

verdicts.claim: The levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) from large hydropower is roughly $30-60/MWh (0.03-0.06 USD/kWh), and far-western Chinese hydro can be at the low end.
verdicts.bestEstimate: Typical new large hydro LCOE ~$40-60/MWh (0.04-0.06 USD/kWh), with the global weighted average ~$57/MWh in 2023-2024; full project-level spread is much wider (~$20-190/MWh). Chinese large hydro averages ~$40/MWh (0.04 USD/kWh), among the lowest-cost regions globally, so the claim that far-western Chinese hydro sits at the low end is directionally correct.
verdicts.reasoning: I independently re-derived this primarily from IRENA's Renewable Power Generation Costs reports (2023 and 2024 editions) and IRENA's Hydropower Costs database, cross-checked against Chinese on-grid tariff data. Key findings: (1) IRENA's global weighted-average LCOE for newly commissioned hydropower was 0.061 USD/kWh (2022), 0.057 USD/kWh (2023, $57/MWh), and ~0.057 USD/kWh (2024). This sits at the TOP of the claimed $30-60 band, so the claim's range is slightly optimistic as a description of the global average -- $30-60 better describes low-cost regions than the world average. (2) IRENA's regional decomposition for large hydro commissioned over the past decade: China and Brazil ~0.040 USD/kWh ($40/MWh); North America ~0.080 USD/kWh ($80/MWh); Europe ~0.120 USD/kWh ($120/MWh). This strongly confirms China is among the lowest-cost hydro regions, supporting the second half of the claim. (3) Project-level range is very wide -- IRENA's cost analysis cites roughly $0.02-0.19/kWh ($20-190/MWh) at a 10% cost of capital, so $30-60/MWh captures the central/typical band but not the full distribution; remote, high-civil-works, or storage-heavy projects (including some far-western Chinese mega-dams with long transmission) can exceed $60/MWh. (4) Cross-check: Chinese hydro on-grid benchmark tariffs run ~0.2-0.4 yuan/kWh (avg ~0.29 yuan/kWh, ~$0.04/kWh), consistent with the ~$40/MWh LCOE figure. Disagreements/nuances among sources: IRENA reports the China figure as a nationwide large-hydro average, NOT a far-western-specific number -- so the specific "far-western at the low end" framing is plausible and directionally right but not separately documented; far-western provinces (Tibet/Yunnan/Sichuan, e.g., Jinsha, Lancang, Yarlung Tsangpo basins) host China's cheapest sites due to high head and large unit sizes, but newer remote mega-projects can carry higher capital and transmission costs. The $30-60/MWh figure also assumes a moderate discount rate (~7-10%); at higher WACC, capital-intensive hydro LCOE rises substantially. Bottom line: the claim is supported as a typical-range statement, with the caveat that the global average is near the top of the range and the very low end (~$30/MWh) applies mainly to favorable, already-developed Chinese/Brazilian sites rather than new far-western mega-projects universally.

verdicts.claim: UHVDC long-distance transmission loses on the order of ~1.5% per 1000 km (roughly 5-10% over 2000-3000 km) and adds on the order of $0.01-0.03/kWh in levelized transmission cost.
verdicts.bestEstimate: Line losses: ~2.5-3.5% per 1000 km for typical ±800 kV UHVDC (1.5% per 1000 km is achievable ONLY at the world-leading ±1100 kV class, e.g. Changji-Guquan; general HVDC is ~3.5%/1000 km). PLUS a distance-independent converter-station loss of ~1.4-1.6% total (both ends combined, ~0.7-0.8% each). Realistic total over 2000-3000 km: roughly 6-10% (e.g. Xiangjiaba-Shanghai ±800 kV ~2000 km, ~7200 MW: under 7% total). Levelized transmission cost: ~$0.005-0.03/kWh, depending heavily on voltage, utilization and distance; ~$0.01-0.02/kWh is a fair central figure for well-utilized UHVDC, but a peer-reviewed 500 kV HVDC study reaches ~$0.026/kWh per 1000 km (~$0.04/kWh over 1000 miles).
verdicts.reasoning:
I re-derived each component independently and found the claim directionally right but optimistic and conflated on the loss figure, while the cost figure is broadly defensible.

LOSS PER 1000 km: The 1.5%/1000 km number is real but cherry-picked: it is the headline efficiency of the world's first and highest-voltage line, the ±1100 kV Changji-Guquan project (3324 km, 12 GW), reported as 1.5%/1000 km and "less than 1/4 of a ±500 kV line." Treating this as representative of "UHVDC" generally is an overstatement. Independent benchmarks: Wikipedia and World Nuclear Association both cite ~3.5%/1000 km for general HVDC and 2.6% over 800 km (~3.25%/1000 km) for ±800 kV. Engineering sources put ±800 kV in a 2.5-4%/1000 km range (line only). So the typical ±800 kV UHVDC is ~2-2.5x the claimed 1.5%.

OMITTED CONVERTER LOSSES: The claim's per-km framing hides a critical, distance-independent term. AC/DC converter stations lose ~0.7-0.8% per end (National Grid), i.e. ~1.4-1.6% total round-trip regardless of length. This is why short links look bad on a %/1000-km basis and why the 1.5%/1000-km figure cannot simply be multiplied by distance.

TOTAL OVER 2000-3000 km: Here the claim's 5-10% band is reasonable and lands near reality, but for the right reasons only after adding converters. Xiangjiaba-Shanghai (±800 kV, ~2000 km, up to 7200 MW) is documented at under 7% total. Decomposing: ~2%/1000 km line at moderate load x2 = ~4% + ~1.5% converters ~ 5.5%, rising toward 7%+ at full load. The claim's stated 1.5%/1000 km would predict only ~3-4.5% line loss over 2000-3000 km, which would be too low without converters; the 5-10% total band quietly already absorbs the converter term the per-km figure ignored. So the two halves of the loss claim are internally inconsistent unless converter losses are folded into the second.

COST: $0.01-0.03/kWh is a defensible order-of-magnitude for levelized transmission cost. Real anchors: the peer-reviewed iScience paper (DeSantis et al. 2021) models 500 kV HVDC at ~$41.5/MWh per 1000 miles (~$0.026/kWh per 1000 km) - at/above the top of the band, and for a lower-voltage, lossy (12.9%/1000 mi) case. Clean Line Energy quoted ~$0.02/kWh all-in over 750 miles (developer claim, not peer-reviewed). Chinese ±800 kV projects (e.g. Gansu-Zhejiang, ~$4.8B, ~36 TWh/yr) imply much lower unit costs (sub-$0.01/kWh) because of very high utilization and amortization. So the band is correct but conflates per-1000-km cost with total cost: higher-voltage, well-loaded UHVDC sits at the low end (~$0.005-0.015/kWh), while lower-voltage or per-1000-km figures can exceed $0.03.

WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE: Loss per 1000 km ranges from 1.5% (±1100 kV best case) to 3.5% (general HVDC) to ~8%/1000 km equivalent (heavily-loaded 500 kV in the iScience study) - a 5x spread driven by voltage and loading. Cost spans roughly $0.005 to $0.04/kWh depending on voltage, utilization, distance and whether converter capex is included. Net: the claim is right in spirit (UHVDC is low-loss and adds 1-3 cents/kWh) but the 1.5%/1000 km loss figure is best-case not typical, and it omits the ~1.5% fixed converter-station loss.

verdicts.claim: Datacenter-level energy per LLM output token is on the order of 0.3-4 Joules/token, i.e. roughly 1-10 million output tokens per kWh, depending on model size and batching.
verdicts.bestEstimate: For mainstream, well-batched, non-reasoning inference on modern hardware (2024-2025), roughly 0.3-4 J/output token at the datacenter level is a defensible central range (~0.9-12 million output tokens/kWh). GPU-only optimized figures dip to ~0.15-0.4 J/token (>=9 million tokens/kWh). BUT the claimed range understates the high end: very large frontier models at high throughput reach ~40-120 J/token (~30k-90k tokens/kWh), and reasoning/test-time-scaling workloads multiply per-token energy 10-100x. A fairer all-in range is ~0.2 J/token (best case) to ~50-100+ J/token (frontier/reasoning, with overhead).
verdicts.reasoning: I independently re-derived and cross-checked the numbers rather than trusting the claim. (1) Epoch AI (Josh You, 2025) estimates 0.3 Wh per ~500-token GPT-4o query at the cluster level (200B params/100B active MoE, H100 at 700W TDP x 70% power-util x ~1500W cluster-incl-overhead, 10% MFU). I recomputed: 0.3 Wh = 1080 J / 500 tokens = ~2.16 J/token = ~1.67 million tokens/kWh -- squarely inside the claimed range. (One auto-summary mis-stated this as 0.6 mJ/token; that is an arithmetic error -- the paper's own inputs give ~2 J/token.) (2) 'Where Do the Joules Go?' (arXiv 2601.22076) measures 0.15-0.31 J/token (Qwen3-32B) and ~0.4 J/token (Qwen3-235B FP8), GPU-only at large batch. (3) Lin 2025: 0.39 J/token (Llama3-70B FP8, 8xH100, batch 128, GPU-only). (4) Samsi 2023: ~3.5 J/token (LLaMA-65B, A100/V100) -- the historical upper bound of the claim. So the lower/middle of the claim is well supported. WHERE THE CLAIM IS OVERSIMPLIFIED / WRONG AT THE TOP END: TokenPowerBench (arXiv 2512.03024) reports 40-60 J/token for 405B-480B frontier models (Llama-3 405B, Falcon 180B, Qwen 480B) on 16xH100 under high-throughput load; Li 2023 reports ~120 J/token with realistic SLOs/overhead. Multiple sources (arXiv 2509.20241; Cell/Joule 2026) emphasize reasoning/test-time scaling multiplies per-token energy 10-100x; Epoch's own long-query estimate is 4.32 Wh (~13x baseline). SCOPE CAVEAT: the lowest figures (0.15-0.4 J/token) are GPU-only; AI accelerators are only ~50-70% of datacenter energy, and datacenter PUE adds ~10-30%, so full datacenter values are ~1.4-2x the GPU-only numbers -- which is exactly what pushes optimized cases up toward the claim's center. Net: the order-of-magnitude and the dependence on model size/batching are correct, and the range is right for typical optimized inference, but the 4 J/token ceiling is too low for frontier and reasoning workloads by 1-2 orders of magnitude.

verdicts.claim: Global LLM token throughput in 2025 is on the order of 10^16 to 10^17 tokens per year and growing rapidly.
verdicts.bestEstimate: Roughly 1.5 x 10^16 to 2 x 10^16 tokens/year as a late-2025 run-rate for major commercial LLM/API inference (input + output + reasoning + multimodal tokens). The true value sits near the BOTTOM of the claimed 10^16–10^17 band, not the middle. Earlier in 2025 it was lower (order 10^15/month aggregate, ~10^16/yr run-rate), so a full-year 2025 cumulative total is likely ~0.7–1.5 x 10^16 tokens, with the exit run-rate ~1.8–2.4 x 10^16/yr. Includes large measurement uncertainty (factor of ~2-3).
verdicts.reasoning: I re-derived the figure bottom-up from disclosed provider numbers, all converted to a common basis. Google (the largest single discloser): 980 trillion tokens/month in July 2025 and 1.3 quadrillion (1.3x10^15)/month by Oct 2025 -> annualized 1.2-1.6x10^16/yr ALONE. Microsoft Azure/Foundry: ~50 trillion (5x10^13)/month -> ~6x10^14/yr. OpenAI: 6 billion tokens/min disclosed at Oct 2025 DevDay; I verified 6x10^9 x 60 x 24 x 30 = 2.6x10^14/month (~260T/mo, matching Beth Kindig's independent calc) -> ~3.1x10^15/yr. A multi-source aggregate (Fireworks AI citing Menlo Ventures' 2025 Mid-Year LLM Market Update plus OpenAI/Google announcements) puts the TOTAL LLM API market at ~1.5 quadrillion tokens/month = 50 trillion/day -> ~1.8x10^16/yr. These independent lines converge on ~1.5-2x10^16 tokens/yr as a late-2025 run-rate. That lands inside the claimed 10^16-10^17 range but at its LOWER edge; nothing I found supports the upper end (10^17 ~= 100 quadrillion/yr ~= 8 quadrillion/month) for 2025 - that would require ~6x current aggregate estimates. The "growing rapidly" clause is strongly supported: Google alone went from 9.7T/month (Apr 2024) to 1.3 quadrillion/month (Oct 2025), ~130x in ~18 months; OpenAI cites 20x in two years; Microsoft 5x YoY. WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE / CAVEATS: (1) Scope ambiguity - Google's figure spans all surfaces (Search/AI Overviews, Gemini app, Vertex API) and is not broken down; The Decoder and Tomasz Tunguz argue it is partly "window dressing" because reasoning models (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Flash) emit ~17x more internal tokens per request, so token counts overstate genuine user activity. (2) "Throughput/processed" mostly means input+output+reasoning+multimodal tokens, NOT just generated output text - if the claim meant only generated output tokens, the figure would be several-fold lower. (3) OpenAI/Anthropic/Chinese-provider numbers are partly estimated ("from thin air" per Tunguz), and OpenRouter's headline "100T" is cumulative ~2-year PLATFORM data, not a global annual figure - easy to misread. (4) No official, audited global total exists; all aggregates are estimates with ~2-3x uncertainty. Net: the claim's order-of-magnitude and direction are correct and defensible, but it is slightly generous on the high side - a tighter statement would be "~10^16 tokens/year in 2025, approaching ~2x10^16 by year-end."

verdicts.claim: Primary aluminum smelting embodies roughly 13-16 kWh of electricity per kg, and stranded hydropower has historically been monetized by siting smelters at the resource (Iceland, Norway).
verdicts.bestEstimate: Smelting (Hall-Héroult electrolysis + smelter auxiliaries, AC basis): ~13-15.5 kWh/kg for most modern smelters; global average ~14.0-14.2 kWh/kg (IAI 2018-2021). Best/newest cells ~12.5-13 kWh/kg; worst legacy smelters up to ~17-20 kWh/kg. Thermodynamic minimum ~6.2 kWh/kg. Iceland/Norway siting of smelters at hydropower: confirmed historical fact.
verdicts.reasoning: I checked both halves independently. (1) Energy intensity: Multiple sources converge on the claim's range. Wikipedia's Hall-Héroult entry gives a theoretical minimum of 6.23 kWh/kg and a typical industrial figure of 15.37 kWh/kg. The International Aluminium Institute (the authoritative industry statistician) reports a global average AC smelting power consumption of ~14,100 kWh/tonne (=14.1 kWh/kg) for recent years (Statista cites ~14,114 kWh/t for 2021; another source gives 14.2 kWh/kg world average for 2018). Industry/engineering sources state best smelters ~13 kWh/kg, world average ~15 kWh/kg, newest cells ~12.5 kWh/kg, and least-efficient up to ~20 kWh/kg. So the claim's '13-16 kWh/kg' is an accurate central band for modern primary smelting, though it slightly understates the worst legacy plants and is marginally above the very best. Two important scope caveats where a careless reader could be misled: (a) this is the electrolysis + auxiliaries (AC smelter gate) figure, NOT cradle-to-gate energy — adding alumina (Bayer) refining and anode/carbon production roughly doubles or more the total primary energy, so '13-16 kWh/kg' is correct ONLY for the smelting step, which the claim does correctly say; (b) AC vs DC basis differ by a few percent (DC excludes rectification/auxiliary losses). Sources broadly agree; the main 'disagreement' is just where one draws the efficiency distribution tails. (2) Stranded/remote hydropower monetized via co-located smelters: well documented. Norway's electrometallurgical industry, including aluminium, was built around 1900-1905 (Norsk Hydro era) on remote hydropower; Iceland followed in the 1920s-30s and built aluminium smelters explicitly to monetize otherwise-unexportable hydro/geothermal energy (ISAL/Straumsvík 1969 by Alusuisse; Alcoa Fjarðaál 2008 powered by the dedicated 690 MW Kárahnjúkar station). Iceland today devotes ~70%+ of its electricity to power-intensive industry, dominated by aluminium, each major smelter paired with hydropower. The 'monetize stranded energy by siting the load at the resource' framing is exactly the historical pattern, and is the same logic later invoked for bitcoin mining in Iceland.

synth.centralThesis: Stranded clean electricity at remote mega-sites such as the ~60 GW / ~300 TWh-per-year Yarlung Tsangpo project should be exported not as electrons over lossy ultra-long-distance transmission, nor wasted as curtailment, but as AI inference (tokens) over fiber, because compute embeds energy at roughly 10 to 1,000 times the value density of either electrons or 20th-century "canned electricity" such as aluminum.
synth.novelty: Prior framings treat stranded clean power as a transmission problem (build more UHVDC) or AI's energy use as a sustainability liability (data centers as a growing load to be decarbonized). We invert both: we recast the data center as an energy-export terminal and the token as the highest-value-density carrier yet found for stranded electricity, extending the century-old "congealed electricity" logic of siting aluminum smelters at remote hydro (Iceland, Norway, Pacific Northwest, Quebec) into the information age. Timeliness is sharp and multi-pronged: (1) the Yarlung Tsangpo project broke ground July 2025 with no published power-evacuation plan and Tibet's local demand (~12-13 TWh) is ~4% of its output; (2) west-China curtailment spiked in H1 2025 (Tibet wind 30.2%, solar 33.9%); (3) frontier inference energy intensity is now credibly bottom-up quantified (~0.3-4 J/token, Epoch AI 2025 / Joule 2026); and (4) global token throughput just crossed ~10^16/yr and is growing several-fold annually (Google 3.2 quadrillion tokens/month, May 2026). For the first time the electricity-per-token, the stranded resource, and the global demand are all large and measured enough to compare directly, which no prior Perspective has done quantitatively.
synth.workedExample:
YARLUNG TSANGPO / MEDOG WORKED EXAMPLE (60 GW, 300 TWh/yr, COD ~2033).

Step 0 — Site. 60 GW installed, 300 TWh/yr (3x Three Gorges), CF 57%. Busbar LCOE C_src = $0.040/kWh central (range $0.030 China-low to $0.057 global-avg/remote). Tibet local demand only ~12-13 TWh/yr, so >95% of output must leave the plateau; nearest eastern load centers are >2,000 km away. H1 2025 Tibet curtailment already 30-34%, so the counterfactual to a buyer is partly *waste*, not sale.

Step 1 — Electron export (Path A). Over ~2,500 km UHVDC: losses ~8% central; levelized adder ~$0.020/kWh at design utilization, but realistically ~$0.036/kWh at ~56% utilization (the historical norm for new west-China lines feeding a variable-but-here-firm source). Delivered cost ~$0.063/kWh; the exported product is a commodity kWh worth ~$0.05-0.08 at destination. Net exportable value density: ~$0.05-0.08 per source kWh. Transmission capex for ~60 GW of evacuation: multiple +/-800-1,100 kV corridors at ~$0.6/W => order $36B+ of dedicated lines, stranded if under-utilized.

Step 2 — Token export (Path B). Co-locate compute; export over fiber (energy cost of fiber transport is negligible). Useful tokens/kWh T at central epsilon=2.2 J/tok => 1.64M tokens/kWh. Electricity contributes c_elec = $0.024 per million tokens. Sold even at the cheapest 2026 budget price (~$0.40/Mtok), gross value is ~$0.66 per source kWh; at mid-tier ($15/Mtok), ~$25/kWh; at frontier ($75/Mtok), ~$123/kWh. Even net of the ~93-95% of revenue that pays for chips/facility/labor, residual value per kWh dwarfs the $0.05-0.08 of electron export.

Step 3 — Total output and global share (SENSITIVITY TO epsilon, the dominant uncertainty).
- epsilon = 0.7 J/tok (best-case batched): 1.5e18 tokens/yr => ~30-86x global throughput.
- epsilon = 2.2 J/tok (Epoch central): 4.9e17 tokens/yr => ~10-27x global throughput.
- epsilon = 4 J/tok (Joule median): 2.7e17 tokens/yr => ~5-15x global throughput.
- epsilon = 40 J/tok (frontier/reasoning, pessimistic): 2.7e16 tokens/yr => ~0.5-1.5x global throughput.
HONEST HEADLINE: "At today's efficiencies this single site could produce on the order of the entire world's current annual token throughput, and plausibly several times it; under reasoning-heavy, large-model workloads that fall to ~once-over global demand." The claim survives even the pessimistic corner.

Step 4 — The binding constraint (where the example breaks the naive reading). 60 GW of compute = ~40 million H100-class GPUs and ~$2.3 trillion of capex — ~14x the $167B dam itself, and a multiple of current annual global AI-accelerator output. So the site cannot be filled at once; it is a 10-20 year compute build-out, chip-supply-limited, not energy-limited. The correct reading is directional: the *marginal* economics overwhelmingly favor exporting tokens, but realized scale is gated by hardware, capital, and chip geopolitics, not by the physics of the watt.

ASSUMPTIONS/RANGES TO STATE: C_src optimism (remote mega-dam may exceed $0.04); epsilon spans ~100x and dominates every downstream number; global-throughput denominator is itself uncertain (~2-3x) and growing several-fold/yr; market token prices are falling ~80%/yr; transmission adder is utilization-sensitive. Present every headline as a range, never a point.

outline.heading: Title: Export the watt as a token
outline.content: Claim-forward title (<=12 words). Standfirst/teaser: stranded clean power should leave remote mega-sites as AI inference over fiber, not as electrons over wire. Signals genre = thesis-driven Perspective, not review.

outline.heading: Abstract (~180 words, unstructured, no refs)
outline.content: 4-move arc: (1) Stakes — the world is building ~60 GW / 300 TWh-per-yr hydro (Yarlung Tsangpo) far from any demand, while west-China curtailment hit 30%+ in 2025; the default answer is thousands of km of lossy UHVDC. (2) Claim — we argue the highest-value way to export stranded clean energy is to convert it on-site into AI tokens and ship those over fiber. (3) Case — electricity is only ~4-7% of compute cost and ~0.024 $/million tokens; a token embeds energy at 10-1,000x the value density of an electron or of aluminum, the 20th-century 'canned electricity'; at measured inference efficiencies this one site could produce on the order of, to several times, the entire world's current annual token throughput. (4) Implication — treat premier stranded-energy sites as compute terminals; the binding limit becomes chips and capital, not transmission.

outline.heading: Introduction (no subheads)
outline.content: Four-move ladder. Background+anchor: the Yarlung Tsangpo project (approved Dec 2024, broke ground Jul 2025, ~$167B, 5 cascade stations, ~2033) will generate ~300 TWh/yr — ~72% of all 2024 global data-center electricity — in a seismically active gorge >2,000 km from demand, with Tibet consuming only ~12-13 TWh. Conventional framing: an evacuation problem solved by UHVDC under West-East Power Transmission. Why now: convergence of (i) groundbreaking with no published evacuation plan, (ii) 2025 curtailment spike (Tibet wind 30.2%/solar 33.9%), (iii) bottom-up inference energy now measured (~0.3-4 J/token), (iv) global throughput crossing ~10^16 tokens/yr growing several-fold annually. Claim stated explicitly ('Here we argue...'). Roadmap paragraph naming the five moves.

outline.heading: §1 The stranded-power problem and why moving electrons is the wrong default
outline.content: Sub-claim: long-distance electron export is lossy, capex-heavy, demand-dependent, and chronically under-utilized. Marshal: UHVDC losses 6-10% over 2,000-3,000 km; converter stations ~1/3 of cost; the decisive point — line capex is fixed so per-kWh cost scales inversely with utilization, and China's early UHV lines ran 21-56%. Only ~20% of UHV throughput is renewable. Quantify delivered cost $0.053-0.074/kWh and note the product sold is just a commodity kWh. Bridge: there is a precedent for exporting energy as a higher-value good instead.

outline.heading: §2 Tokens as 21st-century canned electricity (the reframing + historical analogue)
outline.content: Sub-claim: civilizations have always monetized stranded power by embedding it in a transportable product; tokens are the densest such product yet. Analogue: aluminum as 'congealed electricity' — 13-16 kWh/kg, ~40% of cost is power, smelters deliberately sited at stranded hydro (Iceland ~64-72% of national electricity to smelters; Norway; Quebec; Kemano/Kitimat; PNW Bonneville). Crucial cautionary half of the analogue: the PNW model collapsed when power stopped being cheap (rates +250%, all 10 smelters idled by 2001) — co-located energy-export industries live and die by cheap power, exactly the comparative advantage a stranded mega-hydro confers. Reframe the data center as an energy-export terminal. Bridge: quantify the value density that makes tokens different.

outline.heading: §3 Why the token wins: the quantitative core
outline.content: Sub-claim: per source kWh, tokens are worth 10-1,000x electrons or aluminum, and electricity is a trivial share of token cost. Present the framework: tokens/kWh from epsilon (0.7-70 J/token); electricity contributes only $0.006-0.44 per million tokens vs $0.40-180/Mtok market price; electricity ~4-7% of TCO (hardware ~60%). The value-density ladder figure (electrons $0.05-0.08; aluminum $0.18; tokens $1-123). Worked Yarlung Tsangpo example with full sensitivity to epsilon: ~2.7e16 to 1.5e18 tokens/yr => ~0.5x to ~30x global throughput. State the headline as a range and flag epsilon as the dominant uncertainty. This is the evidential heart; the key figure lives here.

outline.heading: §4 Feasibility: what would have to be true
outline.content: Sub-claim: the model is physically and operationally plausible for the right (latency-insensitive, batchable) workloads. Enabling conditions: cold/high-altitude free-cooling (Google Hamina PUE 1.09) suits the Tibetan plateau; fiber adds negligible energy and only tens of ms latency per 1,000 km, fine for batch inference, training, agentic/reasoning jobs, synthetic-data generation; precedent of computing as flexible/location-agnostic load (Bitcoin mining as 'buyer of last resort' for curtailed/flared energy — Crusoe >250 MW, ERCOT flexible load, Texas-wind mining studies). Honest gaps: water/cooling at altitude, seismicity (M8.5 design near a suture zone), chip logistics into one of Earth's most inaccessible regions. Bridge: but the deepest objections are economic and geopolitical.

outline.heading: §5 Counterarguments, limits, and risks (dedicated section)
outline.content: Engage strongest objections in best form, concede then bound. (1) Hardware, not energy, dominates — TRUE; ~$2.3T capex / ~40M GPUs for 60 GW means the constraint is chips/capital/time, so the claim is marginal-economic and multi-decade, not a switch to flip. (2) Why not build the data center near demand? — because the comparative advantage is the cheap stranded watt and avoided transmission; near-demand siting forgoes both and competes for congested grids. (3) Latency-sensitive workloads can't relocate — concede; only the batchable fraction qualifies (but it is large and growing with reasoning/agentic jobs). (4) Firm hydro has high grid value — opportunity cost is real where a grid exists; here local demand is ~4% of output and curtailment is 30%+, so grid value is largely notional. (5) Water/cooling, seismicity, altitude. (6) Jevons/rebound — cheap tokens may expand demand, not cut energy. (7) Geopolitics of compute — concentrating frontier compute at one state-controlled trans-boundary-river site raises export-control, sovereignty, and downstream-water (Brahmaputra) concerns; the same logic applies to stranded renewables in democracies (ERCOT, Chile, Quebec, Nordics). Do not rebut to zero; show the claim survives within a bounded envelope.

outline.heading: Conclusion / Outlook (no subheads)
outline.content: Restate significance: the watt's best export route is increasingly the token; premier stranded-energy resources should be planned as compute terminals alongside, or instead of, transmission. Concrete, falsifiable next steps naming actors: (i) grid planners/IRENA should publish a delivered-value-per-kWh metric comparing electron vs token vs metal export per site; (ii) operators should pilot a GW-scale curtailment-financed inference cluster at a curtailed renewable site (Texas, Chile, Qinghai) as proof; (iii) chipmakers/policymakers should treat compute-at-the-resource as a chip-allocation and export-control question; (iv) standardize a transparent J/token disclosure so the epsilon uncertainty that dominates this analysis can be closed. Bookend the opening 'export the watt as a token' phrase. Bound the boldest vision with a horizon ('within this decade').

risksAndCounterarguments: Hardware depreciation, not electricity, dominates total cost (~60% chips vs ~4-7% energy in Epoch AI's TCO), so cheap power at the source improves margins only modestly and ~$2.3T / ~40M GPUs makes filling 60 GW a multi-decade, chip-supply-limited build-out, not a near-term switch — the claim is marginal-economic and directional, not a literal 'replace the transmission line tomorrow.'

Latency-sensitive and data-locality-bound workloads (interactive chat, real-time, data-resident enterprise/regulated inference) cannot relocate to a remote plateau; only the batchable fraction (training, batch and reasoning inference, synthetic-data generation, agentic background jobs) qualifies — though that fraction is large and growing (reasoning models exceeded 50% of usage by late 2025).

Why not just build the data center near demand and import cheap power, or near chips/talent? Near-demand siting forgoes both the stranded-power discount and avoided transmission, and competes for congested grids and interconnection queues — but it wins on latency, talent, supply chain, and avoids single-site geopolitical risk.

Firm, dispatchable hydro has high grid/system value (storage, flexibility, peaking) that is wasted if dedicated to constant-baseload compute; the opportunity cost is real wherever a grid can absorb the power — here largely notional because local demand is ~4% of output and 2025 curtailment is 30%+, but it would not hold at a well-connected site.

Water and cooling at high altitude, extreme seismicity (site on the Indus-Yarlung suture, M8.5 design, 2017 Ms6.9 triggered >1,820 landslides), thin air reducing air-cooling efficiency, and the logistics of hauling millions of GPUs into one of Earth's most inaccessible regions are serious physical risks the model must survive.

Jevons/rebound: making tokens cheaper by tapping near-free stranded energy may expand total AI demand and total energy and hardware use rather than reduce footprint — the framing monetizes waste but does not by itself bound aggregate consumption.

Geopolitics of compute: concentrating frontier compute at a single state-controlled site on a contested trans-boundary river (Brahmaputra, India/Bangladesh downstream) compounds export-control, data-sovereignty, single-point-of-failure, and water-security concerns; the same token-export logic is more benign at distributed stranded-renewable sites in Texas, Chile, Quebec, and the Nordics, which should be the generalizable case rather than this one flagship.

Chip export controls and supply concentration could make it impossible to legally or physically site the required accelerators at a given resource, decoupling the energy advantage from realizable compute and undermining the model precisely where stranded power is most abundant.
openQuestions: What is the true production-fleet energy-per-token (epsilon) for frontier and reasoning workloads, and how fast is it falling? This single parameter spans ~100x and dominates every headline number; standardized J/token disclosure is the highest-value missing data.
What share of global token demand is genuinely latency-insensitive and relocatable today, and how does that fraction evolve as agentic/reasoning/batch workloads grow relative to interactive chat?

At what delivered-power price and transmission distance does token export beat electron export on a full delivered-value-per-kWh basis, and where is the crossover for real sites (Tibet, Texas, Chile, Qinghai, Nordics)?

Can chip supply, capital, and construction logistics realistically deliver even a few GW of compute to a remote, seismically active, high-altitude site on the timescale of the dam's ~2033 commissioning, and what is the realistic ramp?

How should the grid/system value of firm hydro be priced against constant-baseload compute when local demand is negligible but could grow, and what hybrid (compute + selective electron export + storage) optimizes total value?

What governance, export-control, and trans-boundary-water frameworks are needed before concentrating frontier compute at a single state-controlled mega-site, and do distributed stranded-renewable sites avoid these risks while capturing most of the value?

Does monetizing stranded/curtailed energy as cheap tokens trigger net-positive substitution (displacing dirtier compute elsewhere) or net rebound (expanding total AI energy and hardware demand), and how would we measure the difference?

What is a defensible, regularly updated estimate of global annual token throughput (the denominator), given definitional inconsistency between API-only and all-surface multimodal counts and several-fold annual growth?
